Nonverbal natural indication is therefore evident in an animal pawing the ground on seeing barley, a listener moving rhythmically in response to pleasing music, or expressions of face and brow accompanying pain. The relevant issue is how the sign leads the observer, not merely whether its physical occurrence has a cause.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: A complex overlap of causal and habituated indication; source expressly challenges a five-type-only taxonomy.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, reporting al-Sayyid al-Sharīf
records.arabicLemma: قوله كدلالة لفظ ديز المسموع من وراء الجدار : انما اختار لفظا مهملا وان كان دلالة اللفظ الموضوع على وجود اللافظ أيضا دلالة عقلية ولذا عبر الجمهور باللف
records.english:
The meaningless sound dīz heard behind a wall indicates a speaker by reason. A meaningful utterance would also do so, and most writers therefore say ‘utterance’ without restriction. A meaningless example prevents a beginner from mistaking the indication for lexical convention. Convention assigns a word to its meaning, not to the existence of whoever speaks it. Another explanation says that using a meaningful word would give two indications, conventional and rational, obscuring the example’s purpose.

The wall likewise makes the sound’s evidential function clear. A visible speaker can also be known by sight, making the sound’s indication comparatively unobtrusive. The lexical aside gives the singular and plural forms of the Arabic words for wall.

Al-Sharīf says in two glosses that a visible speaker is known by vision, while a speaker behind a wall is known through the sound’s rational indication. The natural interpretation is not that rational indication disappears in the visible case, but that knowledge is not obtained from the sound alone: sight accompanies it. His stated purpose of making the indication evident, and his contrast with the wall-case, support that interpretation.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Historical example includes a cross-page discussion of visibility, sound and rational inference; English rendered as an analysis, not a fully collation-certified source note.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: هذه الأقسام حاصلة من ضرب الاثنين
records.english: The conventional, natural and rational types cross with verbal and nonverbal signs to produce six classified kinds. Their exhaustiveness is supported by surveying cases, not a strict contradiction-based proof that no additional relation is possible. By contrast, conventional verbal signification divided into whole, part and external concomitant is treated as exhaustive by conceptual disjunction.
records.editorial: Distinguishes an empirical classification from an alleged rationally exhaustive partition.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: بخلاف الدلالة الطبعية والعقلية فإنها غير منضبطة
records.english: Natural and rational signs vary with different dispositions, understandings, times and circumstances and are therefore not as uniformly regulated as conventional sign assignments.
records.editorial: Do not interpret variability as lack of any causal regularity.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, quoting Quṭb al-Dīn
records.arabicLemma: قوله وهي تنقسم : لم يعرف الدلالة اللفظية الوضعية في مقام التقسيم كما عرفها القطب وغيره من المحققين ، اكتفاء على ما علم من تعريف مطلق الدلالة وتقسيمها
records.english:
The author divides conventional verbal signification without redefining it, relying on the earlier general definition and division. Quṭb al-Dīn defines it as an expression being such that whenever uttered its meaning is understood because its assignment is known. The last condition excludes natural verbal indication, where understanding proceeds from nature rather than an assignment, and rational verbal indication, which can occur without an assignment or without knowing it. Hearing an utterance behind a wall indicates a speaker equally to someone who knows the language and someone who does not.

‘Whenever uttered’ is universally stated because the signification considered in this art is general. Understanding a meaning on a particular occasion through a contextual indicator is not, for these logicians, enough to make the expression generally signify it. Grammarians and legal theorists may instead attend to ordinary communicative understanding, which is why they also invoke customary concomitance. Finally the definition says ‘knowledge of its assignment,’ not ‘knowledge of its assignment to that meaning’: the latter would restrict the definition to whole-meaning signification and exclude the other two species.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Quṭb al-Dīn's quoted explanation crosses several technical definitions; a compact rendering, not full independently checked translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: كدلالة لفظ الإنسان على الحيوان الناطق
records.english: The expression “human” signifies the *whole* assigned meaning “rational animal.” The word “whole” excludes an accidental reading in which a part of the assigned meaning would be confused with the entire conventional signification.
records.editorial: Example of muṭābaqa and its distinctness from taḍammun.

records.speaker: Source note without independent signature
records.arabicLemma: كدلالة الإنسان على الحيوان وحده أو على الناطق وحده
records.english: The word “human” indicates one constituent of its assigned meaning, such as animality alone or rationality alone. This is signification by inclusion (*taḍammun*), not by the whole assigned meaning.
records.editorial: Source item ends before numbered 21, which crosses to p192.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (signature before 22)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو على ما هو خارج عنه لازم له : كدلالة الانسان على الضحك مثلا ، وانما سمى
records.english:
A word may indicate an external concomitant, as human indicates the capacity for laughter. The first kind is called correspondence because expression and complete meaning agree; the second inclusion because the indicated constituent is within the assigned meaning; the third implication because the external indicated item accompanies that meaning. Each names the resulting indication from its grounding relation. Iltizām is preferred to mere luzūm because the stronger formation suits the strongest relevant concomitance.

Each definition should include ‘insofar as it is such’: the complete assigned meaning as complete, the constituent as constituent, and the external concomitant as external concomitant. Otherwise the species overlap incorrectly when one expression has several assignments. If a word is assigned independently to a whole and to its part, its indication of the part within the whole is inclusion, although the part is also a complete meaning under the other assignment. Conversely, direct use under the part’s own assignment is correspondence, though the item happens to be a constituent elsewhere.

Similarly, with separate assignments to something and its concomitant, indication of the concomitant from the former is implication, not correspondence, although the same item is directly assigned elsewhere. Directly indicating the concomitant under its own assignment is correspondence, not implication. If the word is assigned to the accompanied thing, its concomitant, and their aggregate, indication of the concomitant as part of the aggregate is inclusion although it is external relative to the first thing; indication of it as that first thing’s external concomitant is implication although it is a part under the aggregate assignment.

The author is dividing in a manner suggesting definitions, rather than supplying exhaustive definitions of each species, and leaves familiar aspect-conditions implicit. Extended commentaries discuss the remaining questions; the brevity of this work does not require reproducing them all.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long note p191–192 with multiple complex counterexamples; not fully word-for-word, source translation marked PARTIAL pending clause alignment.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله في الدلالة الالتزامية : لما كان الالتزام عبارة عن دلالة اللفظ على الخارج ولا ريب في ان اللفظ لا يدل على كل امر خارج وإلا لزم ان يدل لفظ واحد على
records.english:
Implication is indication of something external to the assigned meaning, but a word cannot indicate every external thing indiscriminately, or one expression would signify infinitely many unrelated meanings. An additional condition is therefore required. Correspondence and inclusion need only knowledge of the assignment: understanding the whole brings understanding of its part.

If an expression has several independent assignments, or its one assigned meaning has several constituents, a hearer acquainted with those assignments can understand all those senses or parts when it is uttered. Each complete sense is indicated by correspondence and each constituent by inclusion, even if the hearer does not know which the speaker intends. Signification does not simply depend on current intention, since established meanings can be understood without being intended. No single word has infinitely many separate assignments or one meaning composed of infinitely many constituents in the relevant sense. Thus the infinity problem does not demand a further restricting condition for correspondence and inclusion as it does for implication.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Q192 contains full argument with several qualifications; first-pass reasoning is rendered but not a photographic clause-by-clause transcription, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Jalāl al-Dīn
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولا بد من اللزوم عقلا
records.english: An intellectually necessary connection must be such that the accompanying meaning cannot be omitted when the relevant original meaning is conceived—for example, the relation between blindness and sight, where blindness is a privation specified by sight. The author points to Qurʾānic usages that predicate blindness of the eyes or hearts to show the conventional availability of this comparison. Quarrelling over the example itself does not resolve the general definition of implicative indication.
records.editorial: Short historical example; Qurʾānic language and precise account of blindness remain distinct from empirical optics.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله سواء كان هذا اللزوم الذهني عقلا
records.english: The wording may indicate that implicative signification requires mental concomitance in the broad sense, whether established by reason or by settled linguistic custom. Another commentator proposes reading the two expressions as deliberately reporting rival schools: some require rational concomitance, while others admit customary or mental association. If so, the wording would not disclose the author's own preference. The present glossator regards the broad interpretation as more apparent, especially in view of other works by the author.
records.editorial: Alternative interpretation of a reported doctrinal disjunction, not a source-level variant.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله « كالبصر بالنسبة إلى العمى » : لا يقال : البصر جزء مفهوم العمى فلا تكون دلالته عليه بالالتزام بل بالتضمن .
records.english:
Do not object that sight is a constituent of blindness and hence indicated by inclusion rather than implication. Blindness is privation related to sight, not the aggregate ‘privation and sight.’ When a relative is considered as relative, the relation enters its concept but the other relatum remains external. Thus the relation to sight enters blindness while sight itself does not, although conceiving this qualified privation requires conceiving sight.

An objection says that, if blindness means privation qualified by sight, it cannot properly be predicated of sight itself. Yet scriptural and ordinary expressions speak of eyes becoming blind without an additional indicator that absolute privation is intended. The reply notes that this reasoning would equally exclude the relation-to-sight qualification from blindness, leaving bare privation, which is untenable. Moreover an indicator is present: the very attribution to sight or the eyes supplies the contextual qualification.
records.editorial: The cited scriptural wording and the exact grammatical reference of ‘sight/eyes’ require separate textual checking; the source’s conceptual objection and reply are translated, not independently authenticated as exegesis.
records.previousEditorial: Q193 note includes objections about Qurʾānic predication; some intermediate phrasing not independently collated; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Anonymous note quoting Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قال الشيخ محمد على بعد الجواب عن التوهم
records.english: It is surprising that one investigator accepts the answer just offered concerning blindness and sight, yet treats the use of “supplication” (*duʿāʾ*) for “mercy” as naming a whole by one of its parts. Supplication is a *request for* mercy, not the compound “request and mercy.” The thing requested is related to the act of requesting, but is not thereby a constituent of the act itself.
records.editorial: Brief comparison of external relatum vs part of a definition. Authorship follows citation, not whole-volume metadata.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله إذ لا شك ان الدلالة الوضعية على جزء المسمى ولازمه فرع الدلالة على المسمى : وذلك لان الدلالة التضمنية هي الدلالة على جزء المسمى والدلالة الالتزامي
records.english:
Indication of a constituent as constituent presupposes indication of the named whole, and indication of what lies outside a named meaning as outside presupposes that named meaning. One explanation says inclusion and implication require an assignment, and assignment supplies correspondence, so the two require correspondence. Another says they are subordinate to correspondence and a subordinate cannot exist without what it follows.

That second explanation is insufficient. A thing considered precisely as ‘what is followed’ likewise presupposes a follower; it would appear to establish the reverse dependence too. Nor can subordination simply mean later occurrence: apprehending a part precedes apprehending a whole, and apprehending a positive capacity can precede apprehending its privation. More plausibly the subordination concerns purpose: lexical assignment primarily aims to indicate the assigned meaning, and indicates its parts or concomitants secondarily. But a secondary intended stage may occur without achieving the principal goal, as someone travels partway and returns before reaching his destination. Purpose-subordination alone does not prove inseparability.

An objection invokes a word used for a constituent or concomitant with an indicator blocking intention of the whole. The reply distinguishes intention from signification: the indicator blocks intending correspondence, not its underlying occurrence for someone who knows the assignment.

A further test concerns the grammarians’ three components of a verb’s meaning: action, relation to an agent, and time. Hearing the verb without its agent seems to convey the action but not the relation, which requires both relata, apparently giving inclusion without correspondence. Three replies are offered. Correspondence may be present hypothetically: it would occur if the agent were stated. Alternatively, the assumed isolated utterance is not a correct use in eloquent discourse, on which the relevant understanding depends. Or the verb is assigned to action qualified by time, while the relation to the agent is not a constituent of its assigned meaning. Consider these alternatives carefully.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Cross-page long note; the full Arabic includes more qualifications than this first-pass translation. Explicitly PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم : انّه اختلف كلماتهم في تفسير الدلالات ، فالمشهور عند الجمهور ما أشار اليه المحشى ( ره ) من أن المطابقة دلالة اللفظ على تمام معناه الحقيقي مطلقا
records.english:
Definitions of the three significations differ. On the familiar majority account, correspondence indicates the whole real assigned meaning whether intended or not; inclusion indicates its part, and implication its concomitant, equally without requiring present intention. Another account admits a whole assigned meaning actually or constructively and requires, in all three cases, that the word be used primarily for its assigned meaning. Its part or concomitant may then be intended secondarily.

Under the second convention, a word used primarily for a part or an external concomitant is classified as correspondence in that use, not inclusion or implication. Under the majority’s account the same use may retain the latter names. Dependence of inclusion and implication on correspondence is therefore evident under the second definition, because use of the whole or accompanied meaning is built into it. Under the majority’s definition the dependence is less evident: familiar extended use or a diverting contextual indicator may direct the word toward part or concomitant without an actual whole-meaning indication in the intended sense. The author, choosing that account, answers with ‘even hypothetically,’ as explained by the commentator. The full dispute exceeds this brief passage.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Q194–195 report of rival definitions; analysis abbreviated, not certified full translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: مثال الأول الانسان إذا اشتهر في الحيوان فقط
records.english: An example of the first case is the word “human” becoming conventionally familiar as indicating only “animal” or only “rational.” An example of the second is the word becoming familiar as an expression for “laughing.”
records.editorial: Brief exemplification from note28.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولا عكس
records.english: The reverse dependence does not hold. A word can signify its complete assigned meaning without giving its listener any actual understanding of the constituents or external concomitants individually. The assigned meaning may itself be simple and lack the relevant constituent altogether, or no specially intelligible external correlate may be available. Thus neither inclusion nor implication follows from the mere fact of correspondence.
records.editorial: The contrast is the possible absence of part/concomitant indication, not a new independent lexicon.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.20 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: أي لا عقلا ولا عرفا
records.english: That is: no concomitance, whether by reason or by accepted custom.
records.editorial: A very short independent printed note; completeness here reflects source length.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله « فيتحقق ح المطابقة بدون التضمن » : اما تحققها بدون التضمن ، فلانه إذا لم يكن للمعنى جزء لا يتحقق الدلالة على الجزء حتى يتحقق التضمن ، واما تحققه
records.english:
Correspondence can occur without inclusion if the assigned meaning has no part, and without implication if it has no suitably rational or customary concomitant. But merely showing that such an absence is possible does not establish its actual occurrence. Lack of knowledge of entailment is not knowledge that entailment fails. Some accordingly accept non-entailment of inclusion from examples such as a point or unity, whose lack of parts supplies an actual case, while treating implication differently.

Another argument appeals to inward awareness: were a further concept necessarily apprehended whenever any concept is apprehended, we could not think of anything while inattentive to everything else. Al-Sharīf says this proves non-entailment only if that introspective claim is sound.

A regress argument says that if every concept necessarily carried a further concept, apprehending one would require infinitely many at once. The reply allows the chain to close reciprocally, as with fatherhood and sonship. Mutual mental implication does not itself make each cognition causally depend on the other in a vicious circle. Nor does the actual termination of the series require that termination itself be conceived, with another attendant concept.

An attempted repair considers the aggregate of a thing and its concomitant. If the aggregate has none, the desired counterexample is found; if it has one, add it and continue. But conceiving the two members does not entail conceiving their aggregate as an aggregate, so the new regress does not follow.

Al-Rāzī instead argues that every essence has an evident concomitant, at least that it is not what is other than itself. If ‘evident’ means that the concomitant’s conception necessarily arises from conceiving the essence, the universal claim is denied: we often think of something without thinking of another thing or of their difference. If it means that conceiving both and their relation makes the connection evident, that broader evident concomitance is admitted but is insufficient for the stricter implicative signification at issue.

A final objection says that an apprehended thing must be distinguished from others, requiring apprehension of those others. The reply distinguishes being differentiated in itself from explicitly apprehending that differentiation. Otherwise every conception would already require an assent, which the source rejects. The thing must be distinct, but the thinker need not separately judge or conceive its distinction from every other thing.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long two-page logic of non-entailment, logical possibility vs actual example, and regress. Substantial selective rendering, but not full source translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولو كان له معنى مركب : هذا شروع لبيان النسبة بين الدلالة الالتزامية والتضمنية بعد ما بين النسبة بين الدلالة المطابقية وبين كل واحدة منهما ولم يتو
records.english:
The commentator now compares inclusion and implication. The author left this relation unstated because it could be inferred by comparison from ‘not conversely.’ Neither need entail the other. A composite assigned meaning may have parts but no relevant external concomitant, allowing inclusion without implication. A simple assigned meaning may have a mentally necessary correlate without parts, allowing implication without inclusion; the source proposes the sun as a body with light as its correlate.

An opposing argument says that understanding the whole as whole and its part as part necessarily brings understanding of composition, which is outside the assigned meaning; inclusion would therefore entail implication. The reply identifies a confusion between something bearing an attribute and that thing explicitly considered under the attribute. What is understood may be the object which happens to be a whole and the object which happens to be a part, without their being conceived as whole and part. Only the latter explicit considerations require the further concept of composition.

Moreover, if those explicit concepts of wholeness and parthood necessarily arose, they would themselves already be external concepts sufficient for the opponent’s purpose. The extra appeal to their entailment of composition would be unnecessary. Reflect.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long note p196–197; source includes additional objections/answers about parts; kept PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي لا من طرف التضمن ولا من طرف الالتزام
records.english: That is, no necessary implication follows in either direction: not from indication by inclusion to indication by concomitance, nor from indication by concomitance to indication by inclusion. The author leaves these relations unstated because the earlier cases provide enough information for a thoughtful learner to infer them.
records.editorial: Short source explanation, not a new formal proof.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما لم يقل واللفظ كما عبر به البعض
records.english: The author avoids saying “and the expression” without qualification because that would make the subsequent definition of simple and compound terms apply to meaningless utterances, which are not technical simple terms; likewise signs that have meanings only by natural response or accidental association do not enter the intended conventional verbal classification.
records.editorial: Source distinguishes deliberate assignment from natural/rational signs.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما فسر بذلك دفعا لما ربما يتوهم
records.english: The division into simple and compound is not being applied to every object called a “sign” or to the entire earlier sixfold classification. It applies specifically to a *conventionally assigned expression*. Without that restriction some nonverbal signs, such as mere gestures and inscriptions taken under another respect, would be incorrectly forced into the simple/compound lexical division. The expression assigned a meaning for syntactic combination is likewise not the object of the present classification unless that assigned meaning is considered.
records.editorial: Correctly restricts the type of sign to which the division applies.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان أريد بجزء منه الدلالة على جزء معناه : يعنى بالدلالة : دلالة المطابقيّة كما قيد بذلك الكاتبي وغيره لا التضمنى والالتزامي خاصة ولا مجموع الثلاث
records.english:
In defining a compound as an expression whose part is intended to signify a part of its meaning, the signification meant is correspondence, as al-Kātibī and others specify. It is not inclusion or implication alone, their conjunction, or an unrestricted notion covering all three. Otherwise an expression composed of two independently meaningful elements could be compound relative to its whole assigned meaning yet simple relative to a simple included part or simple external concomitant, which has no parts to be indicated.

A commentator objects that being compound under one meaning and simple under another is harmless. ‘ʿAbd Allāh’ is simple as a personal name and compound as ‘servant of God’; ‘rational animal’ can likewise be a name or a description. Why should differences between correspondence and inclusion or implication be less allowable?

A preferable rationale for prioritising correspondence is then offered. Composition under an included meaning entails composition under the whole: a part of a part is a part. Composition under an implied meaning likewise presupposes corresponding signification of the relevant expression-parts. But composition under the whole does not entail composition under its included or implied meanings, which may be simple. Correspondence is therefore the more fundamental criterion. An objection reverses the reasoning for simplicity, since simplicity under the whole entails simplicity under the other senses, not conversely. The answer gives priority to the positive concept of composition over the privative concept of simplicity. This establishes preference for the criterion rather than, by itself, absolute necessity.

The earlier objection can also be answered by distinguishing two assignments from one. Proper-name and descriptive uses involve different assignments, whereas the disputed correspondence/inclusion/implication comparison concerns one assignment and one use. The permitted change of classification in the former case does not automatically license indistinct classification in the latter. ‘Intended’ must also mean a legitimate intention under linguistic convention: arbitrarily intending a syllable of Zayd to signify part of his meaning does not make the name compound; nor does such arbitrary intention alter a multiword phrase already used as a single proper name.

The familiar difficulty concerns verbs. Their material letters appear to signify action and their form, constituted by vowels, pauses and letter-order, time. A verb would therefore have a part signifying a part of its meaning, although it is ordinarily counted simple. The standard answer restricts ‘part’ to an audible component ordered in hearing; a purely formal configuration is not separately audible.

But an imperative or a verb with an implicit subject is counted compound with that subject, although one component is unspoken. The reply extends audible to what is grammatically supposed or capable of being heard: the implicit ‘you’ in an imperative and ‘he’ in the appropriate verbal clause satisfy that condition.

The glossator finds the answer unstable. If form is conceded to be a component of the verb, which is an utterance, denying that component is audible threatens the claim that the whole is an utterance. Better deny that the form is a separately countable part of the verbal expression. This also blocks the renewed argument that the remaining material alone indicates a part of the meaning: once the proposed form/material division is rejected as a division into expression-parts, the relevant objection has lost its premise.

More fundamentally, all these difficulties assume that the verb’s meaning is the aggregate of action, time and relation to an agent. On the writer’s preferred account, it is a simple configuration abstracted from those three. The material-and-form expression jointly signifies that simple configuration; one need not grant that its material separately signifies action and its form separately time. The counterexample then does not arise in the proposed form.

Finally, although the simple is naturally prior to the compound, the definition considers the concepts as a possession-and-privation opposition. Privation is understood through what it lacks; the positive concept is also considered nobler. The author therefore presents compound before simple in this conceptual division without denying the natural priority of simpler components.
records.editorial: This preserves the source’s alternative defences and its preferred account rather than treating every proposed solution as jointly accepted. The philosophical theory of verbal form is reported, not independently established.
records.previousEditorial: LONG three-page technical discussion. This is a structured first-pass rendering of the argument, not full clause-paired Arabic; remain PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: المراد من الجزء ، هو الجزء المسموع المرتب في السمع سواء كان تحقيقا أو تقديرا فيندفع ما قيل : من أن ما ذكرتموه في تعريف المركب يقتضى ان يكون الافعال مر
records.english:
The relevant ‘part’ is an audible component ordered in hearing, actually or in grammatical supposition. This answers the objection that verbs would all be compound because their material signifies action and their formal configuration signifies time. The form is not independently audible and ordered as another expression-part. It also allows an imperative’s implicit subject, since ‘strike!’ is grammatically equivalent to ‘strike, you!’

One may instead deny that form is a part of the verb at all in that sense. A formal configuration, as ordinarily understood, is not itself an utterance; combining an utterance with something not uttered would not make both independent audible parts. Otherwise the classification of verbs among words and their study in grammar and morphology would become problematic.

A further difficulty remains with audible present-tense prefixes indicating person and with the alif indicating participation in the relevant verbal pattern: these are both heard and semantically functional. Expressions with the definite article, feminine suffix or relational suffix present no identical problem, because logicians may regard them as compound; nothing in their own wording establishes that all are simple. A grammatical commentary’s calling them simple may concern their taking one inflection, or simply a different grammatical convention. Grammarians’ classifications are not automatically authoritative for the logicians’ different criterion.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Cross-page condensed argument, source note is longer. Remains PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله والثالث ان يدل جزء لفظه على جزء معناه
records.english: The original Aristotelian definition of a compound was commonly stated as an expression whose part indicates a part of its meaning. Later writers added that this indication must be **intended**, because a multiword expression such as “ʿAbd Allāh” may be used as a single proper name without intending its components separately to signify a servant and God. The logician's attention to semantic unity explains why this case differs from a grammatical division based on word count alone.
records.editorial: The historical reference to Aristotle is a report, not an independently checked translation of the Organon.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله الرابع ان يكون هذه الدلالة مرادة : فيه إشارة إلى أن الدلالة أعم من الإرادة ، لظهور ان من كان عالما بوضع اللفظ للمعنى وكان ذلك المعنى حاضرا عنده ،
records.english:
Requiring that the partial signification be intended implies that signification is broader than intention. Someone who knows a word’s assignment and has the corresponding meaning available conceives that meaning upon conceiving the word, even if the speaker does not intend it. A hearer familiar with several senses of an equivocal word may apprehend them all although only one was intended.

Others make signification dependent on intention. The Shaykh says in the Shifāʾ that a word does not signify simply by itself; otherwise it would have an invariable allocation of meanings which it could never exceed. If ʿayn is intended for a spring, it signifies the spring; if for a coin, the coin. Without intention it signifies nothing in this sense; some logicians would not even call an uninterpreted sound a meaningful utterance. Al-Ṭūsī similarly says in the commentary on the Ishārāt that conventional signification belongs to an utterance used with an intended meaning which the hearer understands. Other possible meanings, in the same or another language, are not thereby what it signifies on that occasion.

Later writers strongly object. Granting that sound does not signify intrinsically does not make intention the only alternative: established assignment may supply the relation. The commentary on the Maṭāliʿ appeals to evident experience that recalling an assigned word evokes its meaning whether intended or not, and an equivocal expression evokes its known senses. A contextual indicator determines the intended one, but intention and signification are very different facts.

The glossator judges the dispute largely verbal, depending on whether signification is defined as passage from word to meaning insofar as intended, or passage without that restriction. The Shaykh and his followers need not deny the occurrence of the broader mental associations; later writers need not claim that every evoked sense is thereby apprehended as the speaker’s intended one. Either extreme would be unreasonable. Compare their formulations with this definitional distinction in view.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Historical Avicenna–Ṭūsī vs later tradition. Condensed from long p200–201 material; PARTIAL, verify quotations separately.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله لكن هذه الدلالة غير مقصودة
records.english: If “intended” in defining compound terms means *actually intended at the moment*, even ordinary compound expressions not now used would fall into the simple category. If it means *capable of being intended*, a proper name composed of words might be counted compound simply because its components could be used independently under another assignment. The proper restriction is the ability of a constituent to signify its part **when the whole expression is used to signify this particular assigned meaning**.
records.editorial: Distinguishes actual current purpose from use-relative ability to signify.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: فان معناه حينئذ الماهية الانسانية مع التشخص
records.english: If a phrase such as “rational animal” names a particular individual, its signified meaning is the human essence together with individuation. The component “animal” can still correspond to one part of that complex when the phrase is analysed under its descriptive assignment. But that does not settle how the whole is being used as an actual proper name. The intended assignment must be fixed before deciding whether its parts make it compound.
records.editorial: Exact distinction of descriptive content and proper-name use; source note crosses p201→202.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يحتاج الى انضمام لفظ آخر إليه في الإفادة
records.english: A complete utterance conveys its intended information without needing another expression, as “Zayd is standing” does. A lone “Zayd” or “standing” generally requires something else. “The hearer can stop” may refer to the speaker's cessation, the listener's cessation or both, depending on the adopted convention.
records.editorial: Short note on completeness of propositional speech.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان احتمل الصدق والكذب
records.english: A report is a complete expression **of a kind capable of truth or falsehood**, not one whose actual truth and falsity are both genuinely open once every fact has been determined. “The whole is greater than the part” is necessarily true, and “the part is greater than the whole” necessarily false, but both are reports because their predicative form can be evaluated for agreement or disagreement with reality. The criterion abstracts from the particular fact and considers the statement as an assertion.
records.editorial: Modal versus kind-level aptitude for truth and falsity distinguished.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي بأحدهما كما يدل عليه عطف كاذب بأو
records.english: The phrase means “capable of one of the two,” not actually possessing both truth and falsity. The disjunction is exclusive in the relevant actual assessment.
records.editorial: A short clarification of *aw*.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: اعلم ان الانشاء اما ان لا يدل على طلب الشيء بالوضع
records.english: Nonassertoric utterances (*inshāʾ*) divide into those not conventionally signalling a request, such as expressions of hope, calling, surprise and certain oaths, and those that do signal a request. If what is sought is an item of knowledge in the mind, it is an interrogative. If it is the occurrence or nonoccurrence of something outside the mind, the form is a command or prohibition when uttered from superiority, a request between equals (*iltimās*) when on equal standing, and a supplication (*suʾāl*) when uttered humbly.
records.editorial: A source-specific classification of nonassertoric speech and relative authority.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.21 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان كان الجزء الثاني قيدا للأول
records.english: The question is whether the second member is **taken as restricting** the first. It may be grammatically capable of acting as a restriction without being treated as such in this particular expression. Restrictive compound forms include genitive, descriptive/adjectival and related constructions.
records.editorial: Emphasizes intentional grammatical consideration.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله غلام زيد ... انما اورد ثلاثة امثلة
records.english: The examples “Zayd's servant,” a modified noun, and “standing in the house” show that a restrictive compound may arise through possession, an adjective or a governing relation. It is not limited to the first two kinds.
records.editorial: Brief argument from the three examples.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان لم يكن الثاني قيدا للأول
records.english: “Not restrictive” means that the second component is not *considered* a qualifier of the first, even if it could serve that function in another construction. The decisive feature is the current interpretation, not whether the example happens to include a preposition or a numeral.
records.editorial: Note crosses Q202→203.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله في الدار وخمسة عشر : وانما اتى بمثالين ، ليعرفك ان عدم كون الجزء الثاني قيدا للأول اما بان لا يكون الجزء الأول مطلقا حتى يقيده الجزء الثاني كالمث
records.english:
‘In the house’ and ‘fifteen’ illustrate two ways the second component fails to restrict the first. In the former, fī is assigned, on the account presupposed here, to particular relational uses rather than an unrestricted universal containment; it does not contain an absolute noun-like meaning which ‘the house’ then narrows. In the latter, ‘five’ is capable of an unrestricted use, but combination with ‘ten’ does not qualify it in the manner of a restrictive modifier.

The examples also show that the second component may identify the intended relational use of the first or may not; the first may be particle or noun; and it may govern the second or not. They refute the claim that every nonrestrictive compound is confined to noun-plus-particle or verb-plus-particle. An additional verb–particle example such as ‘if he stood’ would make the latter case explicit, but the writer may leave it understood.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: The source also argues against restricting nonrestrictive compounds to a name+particle pattern; wording condensed, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: وذلك لكون معناه مستقلا في الملاحظة
records.english: A noun’s meaning is independent in consideration. Unlike a particle, it can be apprehended as a meaning in its own right without the two related terms being supplied first.
records.editorial: Short gloss on the logician's division of words.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الأولى أن يجيء بأحرف
records.english: The writer would more naturally have said “letters” using the plural of paucity (*aḥruf*), since the counted number is ten or fewer and Arabic usage customarily employs a paucity plural in that context.
records.editorial: Grammatical style criticism, not logically necessary terminology.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: انما سمى الفتح فتحا
records.english: The vowel *fatḥa* is so named because one produces it by opening the mouth.
records.editorial: Single-sentence lexical observation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الغرض من وصف المادة لكونها موضوعة متصرف فيها ، دفع البحث المشهور في هذا المقام في السنة الأقوام من أن الهيئة ان كانت مستقلة في الدلالة على الزمان بحيث
records.english: Describing the material as conventionally assigned and subject to morphological variation answers the familiar dilemma. If form alone independently signifies time, then nonverbal words sharing a past-tense pattern should signify time too, which they do not. If material contributes, then ‘yesterday,’ ‘now’ and ‘tomorrow’ seem to meet the definition of the logical verb-like word, since their indication of time depends on material together with form, not the letters in any arbitrary order or vocalisation. Yet they are not verbs of the intended kind. The commentator’s stated restrictions on the assigned, morphologically variable material distinguish the relevant verbal pattern from either counterexample.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: The note gives examples and counterexamples in historical morphology; substantially interpreted, not full line-by-line translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أما الأول فلانتفاء الوضع
records.english: The former case lacks the relevant conventional assignment; the latter lacks the relevant capacity for morphological variation. The two conditions therefore exclude the two proposed counterexamples for different reasons.
records.editorial: Short cross-reference to note54.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما سميت بها لأن الكلم في الأصل الجرح
records.english: The word is associated with *kalām* in its older sense of wounding. A verb indicates a time-related occurrence that changes and passes, so it is likened to something that wounds the mind by its changing signification. This is a rhetorical etymology reported in the gloss, not a verified historical derivation.
records.editorial: Source employs a traditional etymological analogy.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفي عرف النحاة فعل : قيل : ان ظاهره يدل على أن كلما يقال له في عرف النحاة « فعل » فهو « كلمة » في اصطلاح المنطقيين وبالعكس . ولا شئ منها بمطرد .
records.english:
‘In the grammarians’ convention, a verb’ seems to identify the logical kalima and grammatical fiʿl in both directions. Neither unrestricted equivalence is secure. Defective verbs are grammatical verbs but can be logical instruments rather than kalimāt. Conversely, names of verbs are called kalimāt by al-Sharīf while grammarians classify them as nouns.

One may accept the first counterexample, given the division of copulas into temporal and non-temporal, yet dispute the second. Names of verbs do not indicate time through their own morphological forms: other nouns with comparable patterns do not indicate time. They plainly count as kalimāt under a definition such as ‘what can serve as predicate alone but not as subject.’ They might also be accommodated under the present definition by saying that they signify expressions whose forms indicate time, and are consequently treated as though their own forms did so.

The more exact reply follows the present author’s own definition and denies that these verb-names are kalimāt for him. The commentator can also be read as asserting only that every logical kalima of this defined kind is a grammatical verb, not that every grammatical verb is a logical kalima. The defective-verb counterexample then does not refute what was actually claimed. Reflect.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long Q203→204 note with competing definitions; PARTIAL pending Arabic source collation.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وان لم يستقل في الدلالة
records.english: A particle does not signify independently: *min* and *ilā* become intelligible as beginning and end when attached to expressions like “I travelled from Basra to Kufa.” Defective “existential” verbs such as *kāna* can resemble particles insofar as they primarily express a relation which cannot be understood without its two terms; unlike a simple particle, however, they may also convey a temporal determination. The word *adāt* is used because such items are instruments for combining expressions, while the grammatical term *ḥarf* recalls their occupying the edge of a sentence rather than constituting its main element.
records.editorial: A source-defined functional distinction, not identity of logicians' and grammarians' parts of speech.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يرد عليه أن ضمائر الفصل والأفعال الناقصة أدوات
records.english: The proposed identification of the logical particle with the grammarian's *ḥarf* fails without qualification: separating pronouns and defective verbs can function as logical instruments while grammarians categorise the former as nouns and the latter as verbs.
records.editorial: Counterexamples to cross-discipline equivalence.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.21 (quoted)
records.english: Modern editorial reference: al-Taqrīb, p21, discusses ayḍan and whether the ensuing divisions concern all simple expressions or specifically nouns. This later commentary is not translated here.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: A reported critical problem of division scope; longer alternatives remain, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله مفعول مطلق لفعل محذوف
records.english: *Ayḍan* may be a cognate accusative governed by an omitted verb, or a circumstantial expression with its agent and owner suppressed. Its idiomatic use presupposes two things standing in some agreement while each can, in principle, be understood apart from the other. An isolated occurrence such as “Zayd came also” without an understood second comparison does not meet that condition.
records.editorial: One grammatical analysis of the connective *ayḍan*.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بيان كونه إشارة إليه
records.english: The particle signals a return to a preceding division. A return to the same object being divided conveys the sense of return more strongly than merely shifting to a new subject.
records.editorial: Explanation of the phrase's discourse function.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: حال من الاسم على تأويله بالنكرة عند سيبويه اى مفردا ، وذهب بعضهم إلى أن التعريف فيه وفي نظائره للعهد الذهني لا الخارجي والمعهود الذهني نكرة في المعنى
records.english:
On Sībawayh’s analysis the phrase is a circumstantial qualifier, with the nominal expression interpreted indefinitely as ‘singly.’ Some instead treat its definiteness as mental acquaintance rather than reference to a specified external individual, so that it is indefinite in sense and needs no such reinterpretation. The source objects that ordinary genitive definiteness would otherwise lose the distinction between ‘Zayd’s servant’ and ‘a servant belonging to Zayd.’

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī takes it as a cognate accusative governed by an understood action in the circumstantial construction; the Kūfans take it adverbially, ‘in its state of being alone, not with another.’ The present writer prefers a circumstantial qualifier without requiring an indefinite paraphrase, since a definite circumstantial expression, like a definite predicate, is apparently permissible.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Records several grammarians' parsings in compressed form; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفيه بحث : فيه ان هذا البحث غير وارد عليه ، ضرورة ان تقسيم الكلى إلى اقسام مختلفة لا يقتضى وجود جميع الاقسام في كل واحد من الأنواع المندرجة تحت ذ
records.english:
Some answer the objection by saying that dividing a universal into classes does not require every class to occur within every species under that universal. The classes need only be found across the species collectively. Thus dividing simple expression into proper, univocal, gradated and the other kinds need not put every kind within noun, verb and particle separately.

The glossator agrees with that logical principle but says it does not solve this case. The problem is not that verbs and particles lack some resulting classes; it is that, under the assumed account, they belong to none of them. If they remain within the subject divided, the enumeration is not exhaustive.

The correct response is that the relevant unity and multiplicity of meaning are themselves not ascribed to verb and particle in this nominal conceptual sense. The later class-names depend on that qualification, so the effective division concerns nouns alone. One may still object that the original subject is ‘simple expression’ without restriction. The answer is that its division is conditional upon the meaning’s being one or many in the specified respect, as the conditional particle and context indicate. Verbs and particles lacking that qualification are not members of the effectively restricted subject. This final clarification is presented by the writer as an expansion of his earlier brief remark.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long Q205→206 source about exhaustive classification and type restriction; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.22 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله الفعل والحرف اذا كانا متحدي المعنى
records.english: “One in meaning” here means that the material elements of the verb or particle are used in one assigned sense rather than as an ambiguous word with several independent senses.
records.editorial: Single-sentence reported clarification.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.22 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: وجه التأمل أن مناط الكلية والجزئية باعتبار المعنى
records.english: Universality and particularity concern the **meaning**, not the expression considered merely as a sound. A particle's meaning is dependent, and a verb under its complete assigned signification is not ordinarily presented as an independent class-concept in the relevant way; neither is automatically universal or particular under the nomenclature of the proposed noun division.
records.editorial: Source-specific criterion for logical universality.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ليس الغرض من اتحاد المعنى اتفاقه مع اللفظ في العدد
records.english: “Unity of meaning” does not mean numerical agreement between one word and one individual. Different proper names may be assigned to the same individual while each remains a proper name. The unity at issue is of the relevant denoted meaning under the adopted consideration.
records.editorial: Distinguishes numerical count of labels from unit of meaning.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm with separate Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī continuation
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أنه لا بد لتحقيق الحال من تفصيل المقال بايراد مقدمة ذكرها بعض الأفاضل في نظير المقام على نحو من الاجمال غير مفض إلى الاخلال وهي انه : لا ريب ان ا
records.english:
Assignment requires the assigner to conceive some meaning, since it establishes a relation between expression and meaning. If a particular meaning is conceived and a word or words assigned to it, the assignment is specific because its grounding conception is specific, and the assigned meaning is specific too.

If a universal meaning containing relative or absolute particulars is conceived, the assigner may select an expression or expressions for that universal itself: both assignment and assigned meaning are general. Alternatively, the universal conception may direct attention collectively toward its particular instances, and the expression may be assigned to their specific meanings. Their general apprehension through the universal suffices for this act: the assignment is general in its grounding consideration while the assigned meanings are particular.

The dispute about pronouns, demonstratives, relatives, article-definite expressions and related forms is whether their assignment follows the second or third pattern. The author prefers the second, so they initially enter ‘one in meaning’ and must then be excluded from proper names by the further qualification ‘by assignment,’ as the commentator explains.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Cross-page very technical historical waḍʿ debate, abbreviated; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.english: Modern editorial reference: al-Taqrīb, pp22–23, contrasts original assigned meaning with meanings in actual use and proposes istikhdām as a possible explanation of the division. It is not translated here as historical source prose.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long cross-page source with poetry as examples of rhetorical *istikhdām*; these are not fully rendered, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي في قوله وان كثر الخ بعيد
records.english: The qualification is remote in the words “if the meaning is many,” since a word's original assigned meaning in a literal/figurative pair need not itself be multiple.
records.editorial: Source locates a flaw in the alleged rhetorical reconstruction.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لان المستعمل فيه فيها ليس بمتحد بل متكثر
records.english: On the proposed reading of “meaning” as what a word is used for: such meanings may be multiple in proper figurative uses, but then univocal and gradated terms also have many individually applied referents. The restriction to “one meaning” cannot be maintained merely by shifting from assigned meaning to separate applications. A response that the same universal essence is present in all the applications does not settle the problem, since the expressions can also be employed for individual referents, whether directly or by figurative transfer.
records.editorial: Source crosses Q207→208 and explicitly resists the unrestricted used-meaning reading.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله فلا حاجة في اخراجها . . . : لا يخفى انه على الأول يخرج أسماء الإشارة ونظائرها على مذهب المصنف عن العلم بقوله : « فمع تشخصه اى : جزئيته » فيكون قو
records.english:
On ‘there is therefore no need to exclude them’: under the first interpretation, demonstratives and similar expressions are already excluded from proper names, on the author's own position, by ‘with its individuation,’ meaning its particularity. The further qualification ‘by assignment’ would therefore be redundant under this interpretation too. Restricting this difficulty to the last interpretation, as the wording apparently does, is not satisfactory.

The objection applies to the author's words as the glossator explains them, even if the passage is interpreted through a rhetorical shift of reference (istikhdām). It can, however, be repaired by taking ‘meaning’ initially as the meaning genuinely assigned, while the pronoun in ‘with its individuation’ refers instead to what the expression is used for, whether literally or figuratively. On that shifted interpretation, ‘by assignment’ can exclude demonstratives and the like, since what they are used for is plainly an individuated particular.

Two further matters remain. First, an indefinite expression intended to denote some individual or other, alternatively and indeterminately, seems to have one particular meaning individuated by assignment; yet it is certainly not called a proper name. Do not answer that its meaning is not particular by assignment, because it has indeterminate range and can apply to many, like ‘human’ and other universals, and because some writers call it universal. The predicability of many which is absent from the particular and present in the universal is inclusive predicability, not alternative application: predicability of many under one utterance and one intention, not merely under different possible uses. ‘Some individual or other’ cannot be predicated of many in the former sense, whereas ‘human’ can. This also explains why a figure seen at a distance is judged a true particular, although the intellect allows that it may be one among many things. Its actual referent is one personal individual; the alternatives occur in the observer's mind because that referent is unidentified. Calling an indefinite expression universal is figurative, considering its unrestricted range and treating it in that respect like a universal predicable of many. Alternatively, it is considered without its indefinite tanwīn; under that consideration it is indeed universal rather than particular, because it is assigned to the unrestricted universal nature. Understand this.

Second, a proper name can be a name of an individual or a name of a kind. Zayd and ʿAmr exemplify the first; Usāma for the lion, Thaʿāla for the fox and Umm ʿArīṭ for the scorpion exemplify the second. The author's definition is confined to the first class. Either names of kinds must be included among univocal or gradated terms, contrary to the established nomenclature, or they are included neither there nor among proper names, leaving an unclassified middle and defeating exhaustiveness.

One defence says that these are not proper names in logical usage, although they are proper names for grammarians. Logicians attend to meanings, and their meanings are universal. Grammarians attend to verbal rules: these expressions take the rules of proper names, including exclusion of the definite article, qualification by definite adjectives and an ensuing indefinite in the accusative as a circumstance. The two terminologies therefore differ because their considerations differ. Another answer says that names of kinds are assigned to a quiddity considered as one under the condition of mental unity; they therefore fall under proper names for logicians too. Reflect: this is a difficult point on which many have stumbled.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long note with second objection about an indefinite *one of* and names of kinds; condensed, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله اى يكون صدق هذا المعنى الكلى على تلك الافراد على السوية : أورد هنا بان المساواة المعتبرة في صدق المتواطى والاختلاف المعتبر في صدق المشكك ان كانا
records.english:
On ‘this universal meaning is predicated equally of those individuals’: an objection asks whether the equality required for univocal predication and the inequality required for gradated predication are considered objectively or merely in intellectual supposition. If objectively, hypothetical universals seem to be neither univocal nor gradated, since they have no actual individuals among which equality or inequality could obtain. If merely by intellectual supposition, whether or not that supposition agrees with reality, two established rules are disrupted.

First, the writers affirm that ‘human’ is univocal because its predication is equal across individuals, whereas ‘existence’ is gradated because its predication differs. If the criterion were arbitrary intellectual supposition, neither assertion could be made decisively. They should instead say that whatever the intellect supposes equal across its individuals is univocal, and whatever it supposes unequal is gradated, whether the concept is human, existence or anything else. Second, they hold that a gradated concept cannot be essential to the individuals beneath it, since an essential does not vary with different individuals. That argument would fail if gradation meant merely a difference supposed by the intellect: the intellect can suppose an essential to vary too, even though its supposition is false.

The answer can choose the objective interpretation. Hypothetical individuals do not prevent the equality or inequality from being objective. The claim means that, were the thing to possess realised individuals, its predication of them would objectively be equal or unequal. This does not depend on those individuals actually existing.

Thus the individuals considered in univocal and gradated predication may be external, as with human; mental, as with a supposed partner of God; or some external and some mental, as with necessary existent and sun. Retain this distinction.

The univocal is named mutawāṭiʾ because its individuals agree in its predication, tawāṭuʾ meaning agreement. The gradated is named mushakkik because its individuals agree in the underlying meaning while differing in one of the respects to be explained. Considering their agreement, an observer may take it for a univocal expression; considering their differences, he may take it for one expression independently assigned to several meanings. It therefore causes doubt: is it univocal or equivocal?
records.editorial: The cases involving hypothetical or mental individuals concern conceptual predication, not a claim that impossible things exist externally.
records.previousEditorial: A full-page philosophical debate, rendered as an analytical first pass and PARTIAL pending line-by-line source comparison.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (followed by separately introduced ʿAbd al-Raḥīm comment)
records.arabicLemma: قوله اى : يكون صدق هذا المفهوم على بعض . . . : هذا معنى الأولية في كلام المصنف ، وقوله : « أو يكون صدقه » الخ ، معنى الأولوية في كلامه وقد مثلوا لهما
records.english:
On ‘this concept is predicated of some …’: the first clause explains priority (awwaliyya), while the following alternative explains greater appropriateness (awlawiyya). Existence exemplifies both. Its obtaining in, and predication of, the Necessary precedes its obtaining in, and predication of, the contingent. It is also more complete, more established and stronger in the Necessary than in the contingent; its predication there is therefore more appropriate. Under the first consideration it exemplifies priority, and under the second greater appropriateness.

The two differences are distinct: something posterior may be stronger and more established than something prior. Existence in celestial motion and in generated bodies is the example. Its predication of the motion is prior to its predication of the bodies, yet it is weaker and less stable in the former than in the latter.
records.editorial: The two signed voices are separated. The second passage's final الأولية is retained as a reading query rather than silently certified as الأولوية.

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, separately introduced Q210
unnumberedFollowing.en: ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, separately introduced: qualifying the precedence as causal shows that essential precedence is intended. Mere temporal precedence, as among human individuals, does not count: it concerns the parts of time rather than how the concept itself obtains in its individuals. Causal precedence here means that this concept cannot be predicated of some individuals before first being predicated of certain others. Existence obtains in the Necessary before it obtains in the contingent in such a way that the latter obtaining is impossible without the former, because the Necessary is the principle of everything else. It is not required that the concept be stronger or more established in the prior individual. Existence in the generated bodies of our world is stronger than in the celestial motion essentially prior to them. Strength is required only for the other criterion [the searchable closing word repeats ‘priority’; the intended contrast appears to be ‘greater appropriateness’].
unnumberedFollowing.translationScope: Stage114 historical passage rendered separately; not an extra numbered source unit

records.previousEditorial: Long note + a separately introduced adjacent authorial contribution. The distinct quoted material is summarized here but needs a separate fully transcribed source.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: هذا اما بسبب ان المفهوم في بعض افراده ذاتي
records.english: The concept may differ across its instances because it is essential to some and accidental to others, or because those instances themselves differ in perfection and deficiency. Such differences can account for a more or less complete predication.
records.editorial: Short source taxonomy of gradation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, followed by quoted al-Taqrīb criticism
records.arabicLemma: لا يخفى : ان قوله : « ان تفاوتت باولية أو أولوية » ليس مقولا للقول في قوله من قوله كما يتوهم والا لبقى المبتدأ وهو قوله : « غرضه » بلا خبر بل هو خبر ا
records.english:
The clause ‘if they differ by priority or greater appropriateness’ is not the quotation governed by ‘in his saying,’ as one might suppose. That would leave the subject ‘his intention’ without a predicate. It is instead the predicate; ‘for example’ qualifies it, and the wording quoted after ‘his saying’ is suppressed. The meaning is: although the author stated the difference by priority or greater appropriateness without qualification, his intended meaning is difference in these respects, for example. The restricted formulation explains the unrestricted one.

Mentioning only those two does not mean that the author confines every form of difference to them. Otherwise one could object that differences also occur through more and less, or stronger and weaker. He mentions the two by way of example, so that criticism does not follow. — Muḥammad ʿAlī.
records.editorial: A separately quoted modern al-Taqrīb comment, p23, disputes whether these further differences really fall outside the first two categories. It is identified here as a modern editorial reference, not newly translated in full.
records.previousEditorial: Multiple speakers including al-Taqrīb; source argument abbreviated and PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: مثال الأول كالمقدار بالنسبة إلى من ومنين
records.english: Amount as predicated of one measure and two measures exemplifies a quantitative more-and-less. Whiteness in snow and ivory exemplifies a difference of degree in quality. The first belongs to quantity, the second to quality, according to the reported example.
records.editorial: Examples illustrate different categories of gradation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: المراد بالوضع الابتدائي
records.english: “Primary assignment” means that the expression is assigned to this meaning independently at the outset, rather than first assigned to another and later transferred to the present meaning through common use. The qualification is intended to distinguish a word assigned separately to several senses from a word which acquired a second use by transfer.
records.editorial: Source definition crosses into p211.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بان يكون موضوعا لكل واحد من تلك المعاني بوضع اخر
records.english: A homonymous expression may have different independent assignments to its meanings, potentially made in different languages or by different speakers, rather than one general assignment to a range of individuals. A word assigned to one sense in Arabic and another in Turkish can illustrate this if both assignments are genuinely established. The case differs from one general assignment covering many individual applications.
records.editorial: Original example uses *nabīdh* across Arabic and Turkish; language-specific assignment needs lexicographic control.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو لا يكون كذلك
records.english: The alternative “not like that” negates a universal qualification: it need not mean that the word is assigned to **none** of the meanings. The broader subject remains a *meaningfully assigned expression*, so total absence of any assignment would be excluded. This is the difference between denial of universality and universal denial.
records.editorial: Historical quantifier-scope distinction, not merely lexical.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, with following separately attributed elaboration
records.arabicLemma: أي مشتركا فيه بالنسبة الى الجميع
records.english: The word is homonymous with respect to the entire set of independently assigned meanings, though in relation to each isolated meaning the designation is specific. The intended meaning on a particular occasion is unclear without a contextual indicator, and thus the utterance is *mujmal* in that respect. A broader subsequent gloss elaborates why several distinct assignments do not automatically make a word unassigned in the alternative case.
records.editorial: Source note closes before a longer new quotation, which needs its own separate source voice.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله كالعين للباصرة
records.english: The eye as the organ of sight is the first meaning given by one lexicographer for the word *ʿayn*. The source lists its feminine gender and plural forms *aʿyān*, *aʿyun* and *ʿuyūn*.
records.editorial: Short lexicographic item, not evidence of first historical assignment.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وعلى الثاني : اى على أن لا يكون موضوعا لكل واحد من تلك المعاني ابتداء بوضع على حدة فحينئذ امّا ان لا يكون موضوعا لشئ منها أصلا لا بوضع ابتدائي ول
records.english:
On ‘under the second alternative’: namely, the expression is not assigned to each of those meanings initially by a distinct assignment. Several cases are possible. It may have no assignment to any of them, primary or secondary; it may be assigned to all through one collective secondary assignment; to all through several secondary assignments; to all through one collective primary assignment rather than several assignments; or to some primarily and to others secondarily. Negating a composite condition may negate all its elements or only some.

The first case is impossible. We have no expression used in several meanings which has no primary or secondary assignment to any of them, since assignment here includes legally instituted assignment.

Of the remaining cases, the first is exemplified by ambiguous referential expressions according to the older grammarians: they are assigned to the particular referents for which they are used through one collective secondary assignment. You may object that those writers acknowledge an initial assignment to a universal quiddity; how can this exemplify secondary assignment to all the meanings? The answer is that ‘meaning’ here denotes what the expression is actually used for, not every meaning without restriction. Although these expressions are assigned to a universal quiddity on that account, they are never used for it. They are therefore figurative uses with no actual literal use.

The second surviving case is a transferred expression which different arts have transferred repeatedly to different meanings, with use of its original assigned meaning wholly abandoned. Its current meanings have several secondary assignments. The third is again exemplified by ambiguous referential expressions, but according to the later grammarians' account, already indicated in our earlier gloss. The fourth comprises literal and figurative uses, and transferred expressions whose use in the original meaning has not been wholly abandoned.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Long Q212–213 note with multiple cases and subcases, condensed and kept PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بفتح الميم مصدر ميمي بمعنى التحول
records.english: The term is a verbal noun with fatḥa on the mīm and signifies transfer from one state to another. The reported expression “without doubt” has an omitted predicate; in context it emphasizes that the negation applies to the relevant universal claim and not automatically to every qualified case. The difference is one of scope.
records.editorial: Short lexical and logical scope gloss.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله فان اشتهر في هذا المعنى الثاني
records.english: A word counts as transferred (*manqūl*) when its second use becomes sufficiently familiar to convey its meaning without a contextual indicator. This does not require total extinction of its first use. Making abandonment of the first sense a condition would exclude genuine examples where both remain known.
records.editorial: Distinguishes conventional transfer from total historical obsolescence.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يعنى : ان المراد من ترك الاستعمال ان لا يستعمل فيه بطريق الحقيقة مجردا عن القرائن لا ان لا يستعمل فيه أصلا حتى يقال أولا : ان هذا ينافي عد المنقول مطل
records.english:
Abandonment of the former use means that the word is no longer used for that meaning literally and without contextual indicators; it does not mean that the former use disappears altogether. Otherwise two objections arise. First, listing every transferred expression among expressions with several meanings would be inconsistent: if the new meaning is one and the old use wholly abandoned, it no longer has several meanings, since ‘meaning’ here concerns what the word is used for. Second, we plainly find transferred expressions still used for their earlier meanings. Ṣalāt, for example, is transferred in legal usage to prescribed ritual elements, yet is also used in that usage for its earlier meaning, supplication.

The answer is clear. Although ṣalāt is used for unrestricted supplication in legal discourse, it is not used for it literally and without an indicator. When uttered without indicators in that discourse, the second meaning—the prescribed ritual elements—is immediately understood.
