Relative to the original convention, the transferred expression is literal in the first meaning and figurative in the second; relative to the second convention, the reverse holds. Understand this.
records.editorial: Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Q213→214 technical discussion with quotation; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وان لم يستعمل لم يشتهر
records.english: In the contrast between the transferred and the figurative, the second usage has not become so established that it conveys its sense without a contextual indicator. Figurative application exists, but it still needs a sign that the literal assigned meaning is not intended.
records.editorial: Source reports a variant *lam yashta hir* vs *lam yustaʿmal*, not independently collated.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فالحقيقة هو اللفظ المستعمل فيما وضع له من حيث هو كذلك فخرج ب « المستعمل » ، اللفظ الذي لم يستعمل في معنى أصلا ، فإنه لا يسمى حقيقة في الاصطلاح كما لا
records.english:
A literal expression (ḥaqīqa) is an expression used for what it was assigned to signify, under that very consideration. ‘Used’ excludes an expression never employed for any meaning: technically it is neither literal nor figurative. ‘For what it was assigned’ excludes a figurative expression used for something to which it is assigned neither in the convention governing the conversation nor in another convention, such as ‘lion’ in ‘I saw a lion shooting’ or in the bathhouse example. Some say that it also excludes a mistaken use, such as saying ‘Take this horse’ while pointing to a book. That depends on taking use broadly enough to include incorrect use. If use means use conforming to linguistic convention—the principal and most familiar case—the condition ‘used’ already excludes the mistake.

The consideration-clause excludes a figurative use for something to which the expression was assigned in another convention, but not in the convention of the present conversation. For example, a speaker operating within grammatical terminology may use fiʿl for an event without further qualification. It is linguistically assigned to that meaning, so it is an expression used for an assigned meaning; but this use does not proceed under that assignment. Within the grammatical convention it proceeds from another meaning connected with it.

Originally, ḥaqīqa has the pattern faʿīl in an active sense, from a thing's becoming established, or in a passive sense, from establishing something. It was transferred to an expression fixed or established in its original place; its feminine ending marks the transfer to substantive usage on either derivation.

The author of the Miftāḥ says the ending can instead mark grammatical femininity on either derivation. This is straightforward on the active interpretation: faʿīl used actively agrees with masculine and feminine, whether its qualified noun is expressed or omitted—‘a graceful man,’ ‘a graceful woman,’ or ‘I saw a graceful one,’ with the appropriate masculine or feminine form. The Qurʾānic ramīm predicated of bones does not contradict this: according to the Kashshāf it is a substantive naming decayed bones, not an active adjective; alternatively, it is passive.

The passive derivation is less straightforward, because faʿīl used passively normally has one form for masculine and feminine, as with a wounded man or woman. One must suppose that, before its terminological transfer, ḥaqīqa qualified a feminine noun which was left unexpressed. A passive faʿīl used substantivally then distinguishes masculine and feminine to avoid ambiguity, as with ‘a wounded one’ or ‘a slain one.’ But this would apparently restrict literal expression to a simple word, since the omitted qualified noun is kalima, whereas it is commonly recognised that literal expressions may also be compound. One might claim that the Miftāḥ writer does restrict it, as suggested by his definition in terms of a word used for its assignment without reinterpretation. In any case, this is an unnecessary complication: the earlier account of the ending as marking substantive transfer suffices.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله يسمى مجازا : فالمجاز هو اللفظ المستعمل في غير ما وضع له في اصطلاح المستعمل
records.english:
A figurative expression (majāz) is an expression used outside the meaning assigned to it in the user's convention, with an indicator preventing that assigned meaning from being intended. The use-condition excludes expressions not used for any meaning, which are neither figurative nor literal. Use outside the assignment excludes literal use. Specifying the user's convention includes a use for a meaning assigned in some other convention but not the one governing the present use, as explained earlier. The blocking indicator excludes kināya: an indirect expression may be used beyond its assigned meaning while that assigned meaning remains possible.

Some add that the use must be correct, excluding a mistaken utterance such as ‘Take this horse’ while pointing to a book, which supplies an indicator against the literal meaning. That additional condition is needed only if ‘use’ is broad enough to include incorrect use. The author and glossator did not enumerate all the qualifications of literal and figurative expression because their aim here is division, giving an approximate indication of the definitions, not their full formal statement.

Majāz is a mīm-prefixed verbal noun taken actively, from passing beyond a place. It is transferred to an expression used outside its assignment because the expression passes beyond its original place, its assigned meaning. A passive interpretation is also possible: speakers carry the expression beyond its original place. The active interpretation is preferable, since the passive requires an understood ‘by means of it.’

Another derivation takes majāz as a path: one makes something a route to one's purpose, and the expression is a route to apprehending its meaning. The difficulty is that this loses the opposition to ḥaqīqa, so named because it stays fixed or established in its original place rather than passing beyond it. A different objection—that literal expressions would also have to be called majāz because they too are paths to understanding—is not decisive. A motive making a name suitable differs from a meaning required when a description is predicated. The descriptive condition must apply consistently; a naming motive need only explain why one label was preferred when assigned. It does not require every other thing sharing that motive to receive the same name.

Thus Ḥārith, used descriptively of someone who ploughs, ceases to be an appropriate description when the relevant ploughing ceases. Used as his proper name, it continues to apply even when the original naming motive has disappeared. Retain this distinction; it is useful in many later contexts.

Literal and figurative use in verbs and particles is ordinarily considered through their syntactic correlates and in dependence on them, as in ‘the situation spoke,’ or the Qurʾānic expression that Pharaoh's people took him up so that he became their enemy and sorrow. One investigator in legal theory adds that this concerns lexical material: grammatical form itself can also admit literal, figurative, equivocal and transferred uses—for example, a past form used to report or perform, a present form for present or future time, and a command for obligation or recommendation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: عطف تفسير للعرف الخاص
records.english: The following expression explicates “specialised usage” (*ʿurf khāṣṣ*) rather than introducing an entirely independent class.
records.editorial: Very short grammatical reference.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ان كان مع ياء النسبة كما في بعض النسخ
records.english: If the word bears the adjectival yāʾ in the variant reported from some copies, the example denotes *members of a specialised convention*. If without that suffix, as in most copies according to the gloss, it denotes the specialised convention itself. This is a source-reported copy variant, NOT a confirmed independent manuscript reading.
records.editorial: Last H-DALALA local numbered note. Qum p216 begins a NEW section titled حواشي المفاهيم, with its own local note1.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يخفى أن هذا الفرق بمجرد الاعتبار
records.english: The distinction in question is due to the perspective under which the same item is considered, like the earlier difference between *ṣidq* and *ḥaqq*. It does not necessarily posit two numerically independent things.
records.editorial: Short programmatic distinction at the beginning of the new H-MAFAHIM section.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (signature in searchable source)
records.arabicLemma: قوله اعلم : ان ما استفيد من اللفظ
records.arabicFullText:
قوله اعلم : ان ما استفيد من اللفظ . . . : لا يخفى ان المفهوم من هذا الكلام ان المفهوم والمعنى متحدان بالذات ، والمعنى على ما عرفوه هو الصورة الذهنية من حيث وضع اللفظ بإزائها فيكون المفهوم أيضا عبارة عن الصورة الذهنية ، فيلزم ان يكون الكلية والجزئية من صفات الصورة وهما من صفات ذي الصورة ويلزم أيضا ان يكون المعتبر في الكلى والجزئي منع تصور الصورة وعدمه والمعتبر منع تصور ذي الصورة وعدمه ولا يدفع ذلك بما ذكره المحقق الشريف في حاشية شرح المطالع بعد قول الشارح : المفهوم هو ما حصل في العقل ، من أن المراد بالحاصل ما من شأنه ان يحصل في العقل سواء حصل بالعقل أولا ، لان الشئ الذي شأنه محصول في الذهن هو الصورة لا ذي الصورة على أن المراد بالحاصل ، الحاصل بالفعل ، لان الكلية والجزئية من العوارض الذهنية فالذي لم يحصل في الذهن بالفعل ليس بكلى ولا جزئي اللهم الا ان يراد بالكلى ما لا يكون كليا بالفعل بل من شأنه ان يكون كليا بالفعل أم لا وكذا الجزئي .
نعم يمكن دفعه بان الصورة الذهنية كما تطلق على كيفية تحصل في العقل مرآة لمشاهدة ذي الصورة ، يطلق أيضا على الماهية المعلومة المتميزة بواسطة تلك الصورة في الذهن باعتبار حصولها في الذهن ووجودها الذهني والمنقسم إلى الكلى الذي لا يمتنع فرض صدقه على كثيرين وإلى الجزئي الذي يمتنع فرض صدقه عليه هو المعنى الثاني . ( شيخ عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
On the words ‘Know that what is understood from an expression …’: the apparent implication is that a concept (mafhūm) and a meaning (maʿnā) are identical in themselves. A meaning, according to the definition given, is the mental form considered insofar as an expression has been assigned to it. A concept would therefore also be a mental form. It would follow that universality and particularity are attributes of the form, although they are attributes of what the form represents. It would also follow that, in distinguishing universal from particular, what matters is whether conceiving the form prevents [its being predicated of many] or does not prevent it, whereas what matters is whether conceiving what it represents prevents this or does not.

This difficulty is not removed by the investigator al-Sharīf’s remark in his marginalia on the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ. After the commentator’s words ‘a concept is what occurs in the intellect,’ he says that ‘what occurs’ means what is of a kind to occur in the intellect, whether or not it actually occurs. For the thing of a kind to be present in the mind is the form, not what the form represents. Moreover, ‘what occurs’ means what actually occurs, since universality and particularity are mental attributes: what has not actually occurred in the mind is neither universal nor particular. Unless, that is, ‘universal’ is taken to mean what need not actually be universal but is of a kind to be universal, whether actually so or not; the same would apply to ‘particular.’

The difficulty can, however, be removed as follows. ‘Mental form’ is used both for a quality occurring in the intellect which serves as a mirror for apprehending what the form represents, and for the known quiddity distinguished in the mind by means of that form, considered with respect to its presence in the mind and its mental existence. It is the latter that is divided into a universal, whose predication of many can be supposed without impossibility, and a particular, whose predication of many cannot be so supposed.
records.editorial: Supersedes the Stage112 partial English, which remains in its immutable source file. This is full coverage of the digital numbered note, not a photographed witness. The digital wording ‘سواء حصل بالعقل أولا’ and the repeated potential/actual phrasing are retained in Arabic; the English reads the evident contrast ‘whether or not it occurs.’ The distinction is between a particular cognitive quality and the represented quiddity considered in mental existence; it does not establish that every school uses ‘mental form’ identically.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فإن المعنى اما مفعل من عنى
records.english: The word *maʿnā* can be derived as a noun from the verb “to intend,” or as a lightened passive-participial form meaning what is intended. The first derivation is preferred because it avoids assuming several sound changes and deletions required by the second.
records.editorial: Traditional morphological derivation, not independent comparative etymology.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, followed by separate ʿAbd al-Raḥīm note
records.arabicLemma: قوله الفرض هاهنا بمعنى تجويز العقل : إشارة إلى دفع ما يتوهم من انا لا نسلم امتناع فرض
records.english:
On ‘supposition here means the intellect's allowing’: this answers the objection that we do not grant the impossibility of supposing a particular to be predicable of many. Why could one not suppose Zayd to apply to numerous individuals? That seems no stranger than supposing a human with several heads or none. If supposition is included in the division, as the author includes it, a thing seems to become a division opposed to itself, since every particular could supposedly apply to many. If supposition is omitted, the particular's definition includes too much and the universal's too little, because universals without realised instances—such as a supposed partner of God or the phoenix—cannot actually be predicated of anything.

The answer is that ‘supposition’ does not mean merely making an assumption. It means the intellect's allowing and accepting the possibility under consideration. More will be said about this.

Two familiar discussions arise. First, the universal's definition appears not to exclude everything foreign to it, and the particular's not to include every particular. A figure seen at a distance might be identified as one among many things; would it therefore be universal, although it is a true particular? Also, the concept of each particular agrees with representations of that thing in many people's minds and could be supposed predicable of them; would it therefore be universal?

The first difficulty is answered by the earlier distinction: the predicability used in these definitions is inclusive, not alternative. The distant figure's possible identification with many candidates is alternative; its actual referent is a single individual. An indefinite expression intended for some individual or other is likewise particular, despite its unrestricted range. Calling it universal is figurative. The second difficulty is answered by distinguishing original existence from derivative representational existence. The individual thing's presence in several minds belongs to the latter. The same distinction answers the objection that an abstracted image of a particular would place one real particular in several subjects. What is impossible is one particular's original existence in several subjects; derivative representation resolves into several distinct individual occurrences. Reflect.

The second discussion reverses the charge: the particular's definition appears too broad and the universal's too narrow. Suppose a universal applied to two, three, four or five individuals, but not beyond five. Would it count as particular because ‘many’ is alleged to begin at six? This objection derives six from the grammatical claim that a plural comprises at least three units and that the least thing called ‘many’ is two. A further objection says that kathīrīn is a masculine rational plural, so a universal applying to nonrational things would satisfy the particular's definition rather than the universal's. ‘Multiplicity’ would therefore be preferable to ‘many individuals,’ as the author himself uses it in the five predicables.

The first answer denies a universal whose applicability cannot reach six or more: every universal has indefinitely many individuals, at least mentally, and the definition's predicability embraces external and mental instances. The second answer notes that a masculine rational plural, though assigned primarily to rational beings, can also be used more broadly or specifically of nonrational things. Another reply to both objections says that writers on intelligible matters attend to the conveyed concepts rather than the niceties of grammatical convention. One should not be astonished to find their illustrative expressions disregarding an ordinary agreement rule.

The particular and universal are named through their relation to part and whole. Ordinarily a particular is a whole containing a universal as a constituent: Zayd comprises humanity and external individuation; human comprises animal and rational; animal comprises the growing body, and so forth through body and substance. Part and whole are relative notions. The ‘particular’ is the whole considered in relation to its part; the ‘universal’ is the part considered in relation to its whole. ‘Ordinarily’ excludes the property and common accident, which lie outside the quiddity of their individuals and are not constituents. Genus and differentia, by contrast, constitute the species, and the species enters the individual. — Muḥammad ʿAlī.

A separately introduced explanation by ʿAbd al-Raḥīm states the problem briefly. One might suppose Zayd himself to apply to many and thus satisfy the universal's definition. But farḍ has two senses: assumption, as conveyed by conditional expressions, and intellectual admissibility. The latter is intended: understanding the concept does not prevent the intellect from allowing it to be affirmatively predicated of many. An individual's individuation cannot simply be disregarded while retaining that very individual; disregarding it removes the individuality in question. Things genuinely distinct from an object may be left out of consideration without that result. As for the distant figure which might be Zayd, ʿAmr or Bakr, its possible identifications are alternative, whereas the universal is predicable of many together.
records.editorial: The last separately attributed passage contains a compressed or defective ‘لا يقال’ transition in the digital text. The English preserves its intelligible distinction without claiming to restore the omitted objection. The purported grammatical minimum of ‘many’ is a reported objection, not an endorsed arithmetic or linguistic rule.
records.previousEditorial: Q216–218 long source, several objections/replies omitted, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm with further quoted Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī intervention
records.arabicLemma: قوله كشريك الباري تعالى . . . : فإنه كلى له افراد متعددة بحسب الذهن وان امتنعت بحسب الخارج .
records.english:
On ‘a partner of the Creator’: this is a universal with several mentally conceived instances, although external instances are impossible.

You may object that supposition has just been explained as the intellect's allowing and accepting, whereas the intellect does not allow a partner of God to exist, much less several. This would instead be one of the merely hypothetical universals without instances in reality itself, mentally or externally. Dividing the universal into impossible and possible would then divide a thing into itself and something foreign to it.

The reply denies that the intellect cannot provisionally allow such existence or multiplicity. Otherwise many rational people, held responsible for fundamental beliefs and practical obligations, would never have adopted it. Intellectual allowance here does not mean the conclusion of correct reasoning, but what the intellect initially admits before that reasoning. Under this first, unexamined consideration—called the foolish first view—it can admit things whose external existence is impossible.

What, then, of hypothetical universals such as ‘not-possible in the general sense,’ ‘non-thing,’ ‘nonexistent’ and ‘what is absent’? Are they included in the division? One answer excludes them: the rules need be general only according to the purposes of this art, and its practitioners have no purpose in hypothetical universals without external instances. A second answer includes them.

The objection to inclusion is that they cannot be supposed predicable of many, since nothing can satisfy such descriptions without a coincidence of contradictories. The reply extends predicability to both what obtains in reality itself and what obtains under intellectual supposition. But would that not also make Zayd universal, since one could suppose him predicable of several people just as one supposes ‘non-thing’ predicable of things? The author distinguishes supposing an impossible situation from a supposition which is itself impossible. Supposing what is impossible is not itself necessarily impossible, whereas an impossibility remains impossible. Reflect: the distinction is subtle.
records.editorial: The digital closing sentence prints ‘فرض ممتنع’ for both contrasted cases, leaving the intended syntactic distinction unmarked. The following explicit maxim supports the distinction rendered, but the precise wording needs a printed-source check. The two proposed treatments of empty hypothetical universals are not collapsed into one answer.
records.previousEditorial: Extended dispute crosses Q218–219, important distinctions of abstract repeatability vs real possibility; not fully translated, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mullā ʿAlī Akbar al-Ahrī, independently signed
records.arabicLemma: قوله : اى لم يمتنع : قد يراد به الامكان الخاص وهو سلب الضرورة عن الطرفين وقد يراد به الامكان العام وهو سلب الضرورة عن طرف المقابل .
records.english:
On ‘that is, it is not impossible’: this can mean special possibility, the removal of necessity from both sides, or general possibility, the removal of necessity from the opposite side.

Four notions are in view: general possibility, special possibility, necessary existence and impossibility. The latter three can fall under the first when the side from which necessity is removed is allowed to vary. General possibility removes necessity from one side while leaving the other unconsidered: either from a thing's existence without deciding about its nonexistence, or from its nonexistence without deciding about its existence. If necessity is removed from existence, nonexistence may be necessary, giving the impossible, or not necessary, giving the specially possible. If necessity is removed from nonexistence, existence may be necessary, giving necessary existence, or not necessary, again giving special possibility.

An objection to ‘or its instances are possible’ says: if general possibility is intended, it cannot be opposed to ‘or they are impossible,’ because impossibility is itself one case of general possibility. A species cannot be a coordinate alternative to its genus. If special possibility is intended, the subsequent division cannot include necessary existence among its cases.

The answer is that general possibility is intended, but the objection confuses its two directions. Impossibility falls under general possibility which removes necessity from existence. The possibility intended here instead removes necessity from nonexistence; impossibility is not one of its cases. — Mullā ʿAlī Akbar al-Ahrī.
records.editorial: The direction from which necessity is removed is essential. The passage does not claim that one fixed affirmative possibility operator simultaneously includes both the necessary and the impossible.
records.previousEditorial: Separate signed al-Ahrī note, not automatically Y or other later scholar. A complex modal passage, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.25 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أي لم تمتنع أفراده في الخارج
records.english: The intellect does not reject an instance's appearing in external reality. Under that preliminary condition, either one instance must exist while the rest cannot, or instances may remain possible whether or not actually present. The writer suggests it would be clearer to divide the cases explicitly into universally impossible, one necessary instance, and the different possible patterns, rather than relying on an ambiguous “or they are possible.”
records.editorial: Clarifies the classification of universal concepts by possible instance numbers.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: هو بالفتح طائر عظيم معروف الاسم
records.english: The *ʿanqāʾ* is described in a cited lexicon as a fabulous bird known by name but without an identifiable bodily specimen. A reported folk explanation connects its name with a white marking on the neck.
records.editorial: Folkloric lexicography; not a zoological assertion about an existing animal.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو امتناعه كمفهوم واجب الوجود : وبما عرفت من معنى تجويز العقل لا يرد ما قيل : من أن مفهوم الواجب الوجود جزئي ، لأنه يمتنع عند العقل صدقه على كثير
records.english:
On ‘or another instance is impossible, as with the concept of necessary existent’: the earlier explanation of intellectual allowance answers the objection that necessary existent must be particular because the intellect forbids its application to many. Correct reasoning does not permit more than one instance, but the initial unexamined consideration can admit multiplicity. Otherwise people would not have adopted associationism, refutation would not require proof, and the theological purpose of sending messengers to correct it would not arise in the manner described.

A further objection says that necessary existent cannot be included among universals with possible instances, because only one instance is possible, not several. The possibility and impossibility in ‘its instances are impossible or possible’ must concern external reality; every universal must already allow mental instances if it is to be opposed to the particular.

The answer distinguishes two senses of intellectual impossibility: impossibility both under sound reflection and under the initial consideration, and impossibility under sound reflection alone. In the division, the author intends the first sense of impossibility and the possibility opposed to it. That possibility can therefore include what is impossible under the second sense. Negating a composite condition may remove one constituent rather than all. Necessary existent falls among universals with possible instances in this qualified sense. Reflect.

Another answer takes the plural ‘instances’ generically for the kind ‘instance,’ which can cover one or many. That is straightforward for a plural made definite by the article, the glossator observes, but less straightforward for the genitively determined plural used here. A further answer treats ‘its instances are impossible’ as a universal affirmative, because the genitive construction is exhaustive where no particular antecedent is intended. ‘Or they are possible’ then negates that universal affirmation. Negating a universal affirmative can yield a particular negative rather than a universal negative. Understand the scope distinction.
records.editorial: The source distinguishes preliminary conceptual allowance from demonstrated metaphysical possibility. It does not assert multiple necessary existents. Rival grammatical and quantifier-scope answers remain distinct.
records.previousEditorial: Long Q220 source, several scope replies; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.25 (quoted)
records.english: Modern editorial reference: al-Taqrīb, p25, comments on ‘the things known by God’ and an unbounded succession of rational souls in the philosophers' cosmological account. This is identified as a later editorial insertion, not translated here as an additional historical gloss.
records.editorial: The earlier partial summary is superseded by this source-attributed reference, not promoted to a complete historical translation.
records.previousEditorial: Crosses Q220→221; some exact quoted tradition and constraints remain unverified, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فانهم قالوا بان العالم قديم لا أول له
records.english: Those philosophers are reported to hold that the world has neither a first moment nor a last, and that rational souls can continue successively without final bound. This is a potential unending numerical succession, not a demand that every possible soul exist concurrently. The note compares it with the indefinitely continuing number sequence and the unlimited objects of divine knowledge.
records.editorial: Reports the philosophers' cosmological account, not an independently proven historical consensus.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (source signature)
records.arabicLemma: قوله : « اى كل كليين »
records.arabicFullText:
قوله : « اى كل كليين » : يعنى ان اللام في قوله : « والكليان » للاستغراق ، فيعم جميع الكليات وفيه ان الكلام انما في الكليات التي لها مصداق في الخارج كما سنشير اليه .
ثم انما اعتبر النسب الأربع بين الكليين ولم يعتبر بين المفهومين ، لان المفهومين اما كليان أو جزئيان أو كلى وجزئي ، فلو قال : « المفهومان » لربما يتوهم جريان جميع اقسام النسب في كل واحد من الأقسام الثلاثة وليس كذلك بل انما يتحقق بين الكليين بمعنى انه يوجد كليان مخصوصان بينهما تباينا وكليان آخران بينهما تساو وهكذا .
واما الجزئيان فلا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين واما الجزئي والكلى فلا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين والعموم مطلقا ، لان الجزئي ان كان جزئيا لهذا الكلى فيكون أخص منه مطلقا وان لم يكن جزئيا له فيكون مباينا ، فلما قال : « الكليان » علم أن ليس حال القسمين الأخيرين كذلك هكذا يستفاد من كلام بعضهم . والحق ان وجه التخصيص ، الإشارة إلى أن المقصود الأصلي معرفة أحوال نسب الكليات بعضها مع بعض .
وما ذكر ان الجزئيين لا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين ، فيه انه ان أريد به ان التباين بينهما باعتبار التصادق كما هو الحق فلا نسلم انهما متباينان وكيف ، ومرجع التباين كما سيذكره المحشى ، إلى سالبتين كليتين والسالبتان الحاصلتان من الجزئيين شخصيتان وعلى هذا قس الكلى والجزئي ، وان أريد به ان التباين أعم من أن يكونا باعتبار التصادق أو باعتبار الموجود فلا نسلم ان الجزئيين لا يكونان إلا متباينين فان النسب الأربع ح تجرى بينهما وبين الكلى والجزئي . ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
On ‘that is, any two universals’: the definite article in ‘the two universals’ is exhaustive and therefore embraces all universals. There is a difficulty: the discussion concerns only universals having an instance in external reality, as we shall indicate.

The four relations were considered between two universals, rather than between two concepts, because two concepts may both be universal, both particular, or one universal and the other particular. Had the author said ‘the two concepts,’ one might suppose that every kind of relation occurs within each of these three classes. That is not so. All four occur between universals in the sense that there are two particular universals between which disjointness obtains, two others between which equality obtains, and so forth.

Between two particulars, on this explanation, only disjointness occurs. Between a particular and a universal, only disjointness or unrestricted inclusion occurs: if the particular is an instance of this universal, it is absolutely narrower than it; if it is not an instance, it is disjoint. By saying ‘the two universals,’ the author indicates that the other two classes are not in the same position. This is what can be gathered from some writers. The truth, however, is that the restriction indicates that the principal purpose is to learn the relations of universals to one another.

As for the assertion that only disjointness occurs between two particulars: if the disjointness concerns their joint predicability, as it properly should, we do not grant that they are disjoint in this technical sense. How could we? Disjointness, as the glossator will state, resolves into two universal negatives; but the two negatives formed from particulars are singular propositions. Apply the same consideration to a universal and a particular. If, instead, ‘disjointness’ is broad enough to concern either joint predicability or the existing things themselves, we do not grant that particulars can only be disjoint. Under that interpretation, the four relations can occur between them, and between a universal and a particular.
records.editorial: The note first reports a rationale and then rejects part of it; the English retains both voices. ‘Particular universals’ here means two specifically selected universal concepts, not concepts simultaneously universal and logically particular. The treatment of particulars is source-specific, not a modern set-theoretic claim.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (signature Q222)
records.arabicLemma: قوله لا بد ان يتحقق بينهما احدى النسب الأربع
records.arabicFullText:
قوله لا بد ان يتحقق بينهما احدى النسب الأربع : فيه إشارة إلى دفع ما أورده بعضهم حيث قال : ان المباينة الجزئية قسم من النسب المطلق مع أنها غير مندرجة في شئ من الأقسام الأربعة فلا يكون التقسيم حاصرا . وحاصل الجواب : ان المراد ان النسبة المتحققة الموجودة بين كليين ولا تكون الا احدى الأربع وظاهر ان المباينة الجزئية من حيث هي هي لا توجد بين مفهومين أصلا ومن حيث الخصوص لا تكون مقابلة للنسب الأربع كما هو ظاهر ولعل هذا مراد من أجاب بان المقصود هاهنا بيان الحصر في أنواع النسب فخرجت المباينة الجزئية لأنها جنس للمباينة الكلية والعموم من وجه ، لكن التعبير بالنوع والجنس مما لا يخلو من نوع تكلف فان كون المباينة الجزئية ذاتيا لهما وكون الامتياز بينهما بالفصول النوعية دون العوارض كما في الأصناف ، محل تأمل .
بقي هنا شئ وهو : ان الحكم بان كل كليين لا بد ان يتحقق بينهما احدى النسب الأربع ، لا يخلو عن ضعف ، فان اللاشىء واللاممكن بالامكان العام مفهومان كليان وليس بينهما واحدة من النسب الأربع ، اما ان ليس بينهما تباين كلى ، فلان المتباينين على ما سيأتي يجب ان يكون بين نقيضيهما تباين جزئي والشئ والممكن متساويان البتة واما ان ليس بينهما تساو ، فلانهما لا يصدقان على شئ أصلا حتى يتصادقان واما ان ليس بينهما عموم مطلق ولا من وجه فلما سيأتي من أن عين العام يجب ان يصدق مع نقيض الأخص ولا يصدق شئ منهما مع نقيض الاخر وإلا لزم اجتماع النقيضين .
ويمكن ان يجاب : بان المراد ان كل كليين يصدق كل واحد منهما على شئ من الأشياء في نفس الامر لا بد ان يتحقق بينهما احدى النسب الأربع ولا ينافي ذلك بما ذكروا من أنه يجب ان يكون قواعد هذا الفن عامة شاملة فان تعميم القواعد انما يجب بحسب الاغراض المطلوبة من هذا الفن ولا غرض لهم في الكليات الفرضية التي ليس لها افراد في نفس الامر لا في الخارج ولا في الذهن لكن هذا ينافي كلية قولهم : « ان نقيضي المتساويين متساويان » كما سيأتي فان بين الشئ والممكن المذكور تساويا وليس بين نقيضيهما وهما اللاشىء واللاممكن تساو على ما ذكر .
فالأولى في الجواب : ان يذهب إلى تعميم الصدق المعتبر في حدود النسب الأربع إلى الصدق الحقيقي والفرضي ولا شك ان الصدق الكلى الفرضي متحقق بين اللاشىء واللاممكن من الطرفين ضرورة بمعنى : ان كل ما فرض انه يصدق عليه اللاشىء ، يصدق عليه اللاممكن وبالعكس .
ثم لا يخفى : ان النسب الأربع كما تحقق في المفردات وما في حكمها من المركبات التقييدية ، كذلك تحقق في القضايا ، الا انها تلاحظ في المفردات بحسب الصدق اى : الحمل على شئ كما ستعرف آنفا وفي القضايا بحسب الصدق اى : التحقق والوجود في الواقع ونفس الامر بمعنى مطابقتها له والصدق بمعنى الحمل يستعمل ب « على » فيقال مثلا : الحيوان صادق على الانسان اى : محمول عليه وبمعنى التحقق والوجود يستعمل ب « في » فيقال مثلا : صدقت هذه القضية في الواقع ونفس الامر والصدق بمعنى الحمل على شئ لا يتصور في القضايا ، ضرورة ان قولنا مثلا : زيد ضارب ، من حيث هو هو لا يحمل على مفرد ولا على قضية كما أنه بمعنى التحقق والوجود اى المطابقة لنفس الامر لا يتصور في المفردات وما في حكمها ، اما فيها فظاهر واما فيما هو في حكمها فلما سيأتي في تعريف القضية إن شاء اللّه تعالى لكن لما كان المقصود منها هنا ما يكون بحسب الصدق والحمل لا مطلقا خصّها بالكليات فلا محذور . ( ميرزا محمد على )
records.english:
On ‘one of the four relations must obtain between them’: this points to an answer to an objection. Someone says that partial disjointness is a kind of relation in general, yet falls under none of the four divisions; the division is therefore not exhaustive. The answer is that the particular relation actually obtaining between two universals can only be one of the four. Partial disjointness, considered merely as such, does not obtain between two concepts without further determination; when specifically determined, it is not a fifth relation set over against the four. Perhaps this is what is meant by the answer that the purpose is to exhaust the species of relation, excluding partial disjointness because it is a genus of total disjointness and overlap. Calling these a species and a genus is nevertheless somewhat strained. Whether partial disjointness is essential to both, and whether their distinction rests on specific differentiae rather than accidents—as in subdivisions of a species—requires consideration.

A difficulty remains. The claim that every two universals must bear one of the four relations is not beyond weakness. ‘Non-thing’ and ‘not-possible in the general sense of possibility’ are two universal concepts, yet none of the four relations obtains between them. They are not totally disjoint: as will be explained, the contradictories of two disjoint terms must be partially disjoint, whereas ‘thing’ and ‘possible’ are certainly equal in extension. Nor are the former two equal in extension, since neither is predicable of anything at all, so that they cannot be jointly predicated. Nor do they stand in unrestricted inclusion or overlap. As will be explained, the positive broader term must be predicable together with the contradictory of the narrower; neither of these two can be predicated together with the other's contradictory, or two contradictories would coincide.

One possible answer restricts the claim: every two universals, each of which is predicable of something in reality itself, must bear one of the four relations. This would not contradict the requirement that the art's rules be general and comprehensive. Their generality is required according to the purposes pursued in the art, and its practitioners have no purpose in merely supposed universals without any instances in reality itself, either externally or mentally. But that answer conflicts with the unrestricted rule that ‘the contradictories of equal terms are equal,’ as will be discussed. ‘Thing’ and ‘possible’ are equal in extension, while their contradictories, ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible,’ are not equal according to the account just given.

The preferable answer therefore extends the predicability used in defining the four relations to both real and hypothetical predicability. There is necessarily hypothetical universal predicability in both directions between ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible’: whatever is supposed to have ‘non-thing’ predicated of it also has ‘not-possible’ predicated of it, and conversely.

Observe also that the four relations obtain not only among simple terms and expressions treated like them, such as restrictive compounds, but among propositions. In simple terms they are considered with respect to ṣidq in the sense of predication of something, as will shortly be explained. In propositions ṣidq means obtaining in reality and in reality itself, that is, agreement with it. In the predicative sense ṣidq takes ʿalā: ‘animal is predicable of human,’ meaning that it is attributed to it. In the sense of obtaining and existing it takes fī: ‘this proposition is true in reality and in reality itself.’

Predicability of something is not conceivable of propositions as such: ‘Zayd is striking,’ considered just as that proposition, is predicated neither of a simple term nor of a proposition. Conversely, truth in the sense of obtaining—that is, agreement with reality itself—is not conceivable of simple terms or what is treated like them. This is evident for simple terms; for expressions treated like them, the explanation will come in the definition of a proposition, God willing. Since the purpose here concerns ṣidq as predication, rather than every sense of ṣidq, the relations have been restricted to universals. There is thus no difficulty.
records.editorial: The Q221→222 seam is joined at ‘لا تكون / مقابلة’. This note preserves the rejection of the first proposed restriction and the author's preferred extension to hypothetical predicability. Do not substitute modern vacuous universal truth for the author's explicit account without argument. ‘Partial disjointness’ is his broader condition, not automatically the modern relation ‘overlap’.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (signature Q223)
records.arabicLemma: ينتقض ذلك بمثل اللاشىء واللاممكن
records.arabicFullText: ينتقض ذلك بمثل اللاشىء واللاممكن بالامكان ، فاللاشيء لا يصدق شئ منها على شئ من افراد اللاممكن وبالعكس فلو جعلوا متباينين لوجب ان يكون بين نقيضيهما تباين جزئي على ما سيأتي وهو باطل . ويمكن ان يجاب بتخصيص الدعوى بالكليات التي لها مصداق في الخارج وتعميم القواعد انما يجب بحسب الطاقة البشرية والاغراض المطلوبة من الفن ولا غرض لهم في الكليات الفرضية . ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english: The claim is challenged by cases such as ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible’: neither is predicable of any individual of the other. If they were made disjoint, their contradictories would have to be partially disjoint, as will be explained; but that is false. One can answer by restricting the claim to universals having an instance in external reality. The generality of the rules is required only within human capacity and according to the purposes sought in the art; its practitioners have no purpose in merely hypothetical universals.
records.editorial: This speaker offers the restriction that the preceding Muḥammad ʿAlī note found inadequate. Both positions are retained, not reconciled into a supposed consensus. The searchable wording ‘فاللاشيء لا يصدق شئ منها’ is awkward and retained; the English renders the stated reciprocal non-predicability rather than proposing an Arabic emendation.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اى : كل واحد منهما أعم من وجه
records.arabicFullText: اى : كل واحد منهما أعم من وجه وهو كونه شاملا له ولغيره في الجملة وأخص من وجه وهو كونه مشمولا للاخر مع أنه شامل لغيره أيضا . ( محمد على )
records.english: That is, each is broader in one respect: it includes the other, in some cases, and includes something beyond it. It is narrower in another respect: it is included by the other, while that other also includes something beyond it.
records.editorial: The qualification ‘in some cases’ matters; the passage does not assert that two overlapping classes each wholly contain the other.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الحيوان شامل للأبيض وغيره
records.arabicFullText: الحيوان شامل للأبيض وغيره وبالعكس فباعتبار ان كل واحد منهما شامل للاخر ، يكون أعم منه وباعتبار انه مشمول له ، أخص منه ولهذا سمى بالأعم والأخص من وجه . ( شيخ عبد الرحيم )
records.english: Animal includes what is white and what is not, and conversely. Insofar as each includes the other, it is broader than it; insofar as it is included by it, it is narrower. This is why they are called broader and narrower in different respects.
records.editorial: The intended example is overlap between animals and white things. Read the mutual ‘inclusion’ in light of note15's partial qualification, not as mutual total inclusion.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: فان قلت : النائم والمستيقظ متساويان
records.arabicFullText:
فان قلت : النائم والمستيقظ متساويان وليس بينهما صدق كلى من الجانبين .
قلت : المعتبر في المتساويين هو صدق كل واحد منهما على جميع افراد الاخر ولا يلزم من ذلك ان يصدقا معا في زمان واحد فالمستيقظ والنائم يصدق كل واحد منهما على الاخر كليا الا ان ذلك ليس في زمان واحد وذلك لا يضر في كونهما متساويين .
ومنهم من قال : التساوي انما هو بين النائم في الجملة والمستيقظ في الجملة والنائم في حال النوم يصدق عليه انه مستيقظ في الجملة وان لم يصدق عليه انه مستيقظ في حال النوم وكذا المستيقظ يصدق عليه في حال تيقّظه انه نائم في الجملة والمتساويان يصدق كل منهما على جميع افراد الاخر في زمان صدق الاخر عليه وقس على ذلك الصدق المعتبر في العموم والخصوص مطلقا ومن وجه . ( شيخ عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
If you object, ‘Sleeping and waking are equal in extension, yet neither is universally predicable of the other,’ I reply: what is required for two equal terms is that each be predicable of every individual of the other. It does not follow that both must be predicated together at one time. Waking and sleeping are each universally predicable of the other, but not at the same time; that does not prevent their being equal in extension.

Some instead say that the equality is between ‘sleeping at some time’ and ‘waking at some time.’ Of someone asleep, even while sleeping, it is true that he is awake at some time, although not that he is awake while sleeping. Likewise, of someone awake, even while awake, it is true that he sleeps at some time. On this account, each equal term is predicable of every individual of the other at the time when the other is predicated of that individual. Apply the same analysis to the predicability required in unrestricted inclusion and in overlap.
records.editorial: Two temporal analyses are preserved. The English ‘at some time’ renders the contextual force of ‘في الجملة’; it is not a claim that every possible organism must sleep. No independent historical modal proof is certified here.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: المرجع بكسر الجيم هنا مصدر ميمى
records.arabicFullText:
المرجع بكسر الجيم هنا مصدر ميمى لا اسم مكان والألم يصح تعديته ب « إلى » .
فان قلت : ان كلام المصنف في شرح التلخيص ظاهر في ان المرجع اسم مكان يصح تعديته ب « إلى » حيث قال في شرح قول الماتن : وان البلاغة مرجعها إلى الاحتراز وهو ما يجب ان يحصل حتى يمكن حصولها كما قالوا مرجع الصدق والكذب إلى طباق الحكم للواقع وعدم طباقه اى : ما به يتحققان ويتحصلان . قلت : لا شك في ان اسم المكان لا يصح تعديته بشيء لأنه جامد محض لا يصلح للعمل .
واما كلام المصنف ، فيمكن ان يكون على سبيل الاستخدام كما ذكره بعض المحققين ، فان للمرجع معنيان : الأول الرجوع والثاني محل الرجوع والمراد به أولا معناه الأول وبضميره معناه الثاني فالتفسير المذكور لمعناه الثاني وبه يتضح معناه الأول . ( محمد على )
records.english:
Marjiʿ, with kasra on the jīm, is here a mīm-prefixed verbal noun, not a noun of place; otherwise it could not govern the complement introduced by ilā (‘to’).

You may object that the author's commentary on the Talkhīṣ apparently takes marjiʿ as a noun of place which nevertheless admits ilā. Explaining the text's words ‘eloquence resolves into avoiding [error],’ he says: ‘It is what must obtain for eloquence to be able to obtain, just as one says that truth and falsehood resolve into the judgment's agreement or disagreement with reality: that through which the two are realised and attained.’ I reply: a noun of place undoubtedly cannot govern such a complement, because it is a purely nonverbal noun without the capacity to govern.

The author's wording may instead employ istikhdām, a shift in the sense resumed by a pronoun, as some investigators have explained. Marjiʿ has two meanings: returning, and the place of return. The first occurrence intends the first meaning, while its pronoun resumes the second. The cited explanation explains that second meaning and thereby clarifies the first.
records.editorial: The digital string ‘والألم’ is preserved in Arabic and read contextually as ‘وإلا لم’ in translation. This is a flagged reading, not an unrecorded manuscript emendation. The reported grammatical rule is the glossator's position.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله ومرجع التباين إلى سالبتين
records.arabicFullText:
قوله ومرجع التباين إلى سالبتين : المرجع بكسر الجيم مصدر ميمى بمعنى الرجوع لا اسم مكان بمعنى موضع الرجوع وذلك بدليل تعديته ب « إلى » والمصدر الميمى يأتي على وزن مفعل بفتح العين من كل باب إلا شاذا ك « مرجع ومغفرة ومفازة ومعذرة ومعصية » .
واعلم : ان ما ذكره المحشى من مرجع النسب الأربع انما هو بحسب الكمية والكيفية واما بحسب الجهة فمرجع التباين إلى سالبتين كليتين دائمتين ، لان المباينة بين الكليين هي ان لا يتصادقا أصلا سواء أمكن أم لا ومرجع التساوي إلى موجبتين كليتين مطلقتين عامتين لان المساواة بين الكليين ان يتصادقا بالفعل سواء وجب ذلك الصدق أم لا . ومرجع العموم مطلقا إلى موجبة كلية مطلقة عامة وسالبة جزئية دائمة ومرجع العموم من وجه إلى موجبة جزئية مطلقة عامة وسالبتين جزئيتين دائمتين .
فالموجبات مطلقة والسوالب دائمة ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
On ‘disjointness resolves into two negatives’: marjiʿ, with kasra on the jīm, is a mīm-prefixed verbal noun meaning returning, not a noun of place meaning the place of return. Its governing ilā is evidence of that. The mīm-prefixed verbal noun generally takes the pattern mafʿal, with fatḥa on its middle radical, in every conjugational class, apart from irregular forms such as marjiʿ, maghfira, mafāza, maʿdhira and maʿṣiya.

Know that the glossator's account of what the four relations resolve into concerns quantity and quality. As regards modality, disjointness resolves into two universal perpetual negatives: disjointness between universals consists in their never being jointly predicated, whether such joint predication is possible or not. Equality resolves into two universal general-absolute affirmatives, because equality between universals consists in their actual joint predicability, whether that predicability is necessary or not. Unrestricted inclusion resolves into one universal general-absolute affirmative and one particular perpetual negative. Overlap resolves into one particular general-absolute affirmative and two particular perpetual negatives.

Thus the affirmatives are absolute, and the negatives perpetual.
records.editorial: The source's modal qualifiers are translated explicitly. ‘General absolute’ and ‘perpetual’ are technical traditional modalities, not interchangeable with unqualified modern categorical propositions. This record translates the classification; it does not certify the 46 unrelated modal theorem cases.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله ومرجع العموم من وجه
records.arabicFullText: قوله ومرجع العموم من وجه . . . : فان قلت : كما أن مرجع العموم إلى ذلك ، كذلك مرجعه إلى موجبتين جزئيتين وسالبة جزئية فلم ترك المحشى ذلك وتعرض لما ذكره ؟ قلت : لأنه على هذا لا يتمايز عن العموم المطلق ، لان مرجعه أيضا إلى ذلك ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english: On ‘overlap resolves into …’: if you ask, ‘Just as overlap resolves into the propositions stated, it also resolves into two particular affirmatives and a particular negative. Why did the glossator leave that formulation aside and give the other?’ I reply: because on that formulation it is not distinguished from unrestricted inclusion, which also resolves into those propositions.

unnumberedFollowing.ar: الفرق بين الكل والكلى بوجوه : منها : ان الكل مقوم لجزئياته . ومنها : ان اجزاء الكل متناهية وجزئيات الكلى غير متناهية ومنها : ان الكل لا يحمل على اجزائه والكلى يحمل على جزئياته فلا يقال : « البيت جدار » ويقال : « الانسان زيد » .
unnumberedFollowing.en: The whole (kull) and the universal (kullī) differ in several respects. One is that ‘the whole constitutes its particulars’ [as the digital text reads; the subject may be corrupt]. Another is that the parts of a whole are finite, whereas the particulars of a universal are unlimited. Another is that the whole is not predicated of its parts, while the universal is predicated of its particulars: one does not say ‘the house is a wall,’ but one says ‘the human is Zayd’ [the source's examples, with their predicative orientation requiring checking].

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله : اى كل ما صدق عليه أحد النقيضين
records.arabicFullText:
قوله : اى كل ما صدق عليه أحد النقيضين : حاصله انه إذا ثبت ان بين الانسان والناطق مثلا تساويا فلا بد وان يكون بين نقيضيهما وهما اللاانسان واللاناطق أيضا تساو بمعنى : ان يكون كل لا انسان لا ناطقا وكل لا ناطق لا انسانا إذ لو لم يصدق لصدق نقيضاهما وهما بعض اللاانسان ليس بلا ناطق وبعض اللاناطق ليس بلا انسان فحينئذ يصدق : بعض اللاانسان ناطق وبعض اللاناطق انسان ضرورة استحالة ارتفاع النقيضين ، فيصدق عين أحدهما بدون عين الاخر لامتناع اجتماع النقيضين وهو خلاف الفرض ، هذا .
واعترض عليه : بان صدق قولنا : بعض اللاانسان ليس بلا ناطق وبعض اللاناطق ليس بلا انسان لا يستلزم صدق قولنا : بعض اللاانسان ناطق وبعض اللاناطق انسان ، لما سيأتي من أن صدق السالبة المعدولة المحمول لا يستلزم صدق الموجبة المحصلة ، الا ترى ان صدق قولنا : زيد ليس بلا كاتب لا يوجب صدق قولنا : زيد كاتب ، لجواز ان يكون زيد معدوما فلا يكون كاتبا ولا لا كاتبا .
لا يقال : ان الموضوع فيما نحن فيه موجود ، فان اللاانسان واللاناطق صادقان على موجودات محققة كالشجر والحجر وغيرهما والسالبة المعدولة والموجبة المحصلة متلازمان حين وجود الموضوع كما سيأتي .
لأنا نقول : ليس الكلام في خصوص اللاانسان واللاناطق ونحو هما بل في نقيضي المتساويين مطلقا فما تقول في مثل الشئ والممكن العام فإنهما متساويان لصدقهما على جميع المفهومات ولا يصدق نقيضاهما وهما اللاشىء واللاممكن على شئ أصلا كما تقدم فلا يتم البرهان المذكور ح البتة ، فإذا قلت : لو لم يصدق كل لا شئ لا ممكن ، لصدق بعض اللاشىء ليس بلا ممكن فيصدق بعض اللاشىء ممكن ، اتجه المنع المذكور فان الموضوع ليس بموجود قطعا .
وأجيب : بانا نخص البحث بما إذا لم يكن المتساويان شاملين لجميع الأشياء ذهنا وخارجا فلا بد ان يصدق نقيضاهما على موجود اما خارجي أو ذهني فيتم ح الدليل وينسد السبيل وتعميم القواعد انما يجب بحسب الاغراض المقصودة والمقاصد المطلوبة من الفن كما سبق .
ولا يخفى : ان هذا انما يحتاج اليه بناء على ما سبق من تخصيص الصدق بالصدق الحقيقي واما على ما اخترناه من تعميمه إلى الحقيقي والفرضي ، فلا ، لعدم ورود الاعتراض حتى يحتاج إلى الجواب وقولهم : ان السالبة المعدولة المحمول أعم من الموجبة المحصلة ، انما هو على تقدير اختصاص الصدق والوجود بالحقيقي واما على تقدير تعميمهما اليه وإلى الفرضي فالظاهر عدم الفرق بينهما ، فتأمل . ( محمد على )
records.english:
On ‘that is, everything of which one of the contradictories is predicated’: the point is that once equality between, for example, human and rational has been established, equality must also obtain between their contradictories, non-human and non-rational. Thus every non-human must be non-rational, and every non-rational thing non-human. Were these not true, their contradictories would be true: some non-human is not non-rational, and some non-rational thing is not non-human. It would then be true that some non-human is rational and some non-rational thing is human, because both contradictories cannot be absent. One positive term would therefore be predicable without the other, since contradictories cannot coincide. That contradicts the assumption.

An objection is raised: the truth of ‘Some non-human is not non-rational’ and ‘Some non-rational thing is not non-human’ does not entail the truth of ‘Some non-human is rational’ and ‘Some non-rational thing is human.’ As will be explained, a negative proposition with a negative predicate does not entail the corresponding affirmative proposition with a positive predicate. Do you not see that ‘Zayd is not a non-writer’ does not require ‘Zayd is a writer’ to be true? Zayd might be nonexistent, in which case he is neither a writer nor a non-writer.

Do not reply that the subject here exists, since non-human and non-rational apply to realised existents such as trees and stones, and that the negative with negative predicate and the positive affirmative are mutually entailing when the subject exists.

We answer that the discussion is not specifically about non-human and non-rational and similar cases. It concerns the contradictories of equal terms without restriction. What of ‘thing’ and ‘possible in the general sense’? They are equal through being predicable of all concepts, while their contradictories—‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible’—are predicable of nothing at all, as explained earlier. The proof then certainly fails. If you say, ‘Were “Every non-thing is not-possible” not true, “Some non-thing is not not-possible” would be true, and hence “Some non-thing is possible”,’ the stated denial applies: the subject is certainly not existent.

One answer restricts the discussion to cases where the two equal terms do not embrace all things, mentally and externally. Their contradictories must then apply to something existent, externally or mentally, completing the proof and blocking the objection. As explained earlier, general rules need be general only according to the intended aims and purposes of the art.

But this restriction is needed only on the earlier assumption that predicability is confined to real predicability. On our preferred extension to real and hypothetical predicability it is unnecessary: the objection does not arise and therefore needs no answer. The assertion that a negative proposition with a negative predicate is broader than the positive affirmative holds when predicability and existence are confined to real predicability and existence. Once both are extended to the real and the hypothetical, apparently no difference remains between the two. Reflect.
records.editorial: The text's transition from failure of the two universals to the two respective particular negatives is reproduced as stated; its exact dialectical quantification is not silently repaired. ‘Negative predicate’ here renders maʿdūl al-maḥmūl and must be distinguished from a negative copula. The existential-import objection is essential; ordinary modern double-negation simplification would obscure it. Hypothetical existence is the author's proposed repair, not an independent modern proof.

records.arabicLemma: بان يقال : كل حجر ليس بانسان
records.arabicFullText: بان يقال : كل حجر ليس بانسان ولم يصدق عليه اللاناطق مثل ان لا يصح ان يقال : كل حجر ليس بناطق لصدق عليه الناطق لأن عدم صحته ليس الا باعتبار صدق نقيض المحمول فيستلزم صدق ذلك . فان قلت : لا نسلم ان عدم صدق ذلك باعتبار صدق نقيض المحمول بل باعتبار عدم الموضوع لا يستلزم ما ذكرت . قلت : القضية المذكورة موجبة سالبة المحمول وهذه لا تقتضى وجود الموضوع كما صرح به المتأخرون فإذا كذبت ، لا يكون كذبها الا باعتبار صدق نقيض المحمول فيستلزم ذلك . ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
One may put it this way: every stone is not human. Were non-rational not predicable of it—for example, were ‘Every stone is not rational’ not correct—rational would be predicable of it. The statement's failure to be correct would be due only to the truth of the contradictory of its predicate, and would therefore entail that predication.

If you object, ‘We do not grant that the failure of the statement is due to the truth of the contradictory predicate; it could instead be due to the absence of the subject, in which case your conclusion does not follow,’ I reply: the cited proposition is an affirmative with a negated predicate, and this does not require the subject's existence, as later writers expressly state. When it is false, its falsity can therefore be due only to the truth of the contradictory predicate, which entails the stated result.
records.editorial: Translate the actual digital wording ‘موجبة سالبة المحمول’ and ‘لا تقتضى وجود الموضوع’ without silently substituting ‘سالبة معدولة المحمول’ or reversing the existential claim. records.english: The statement is: everything of which the contradictory of the broader term is predicated also has the contradictory of the narrower term predicated of it. The previous objection applies here too. Suppose you say: were ‘Every not-possible thing is non-human’ not true, its contradictory would be true—‘Some not-possible thing is not non-human’—and hence ‘Some not-possible thing is human.’ One may object that ‘Some not-possible thing is not non-human’ is a negative proposition with a negative predicate. It is broader than the corresponding positive affirmative, so its truth does not entail ‘Some not-possible thing is human.’ The answer is the one given earlier. Reflect.
records.editorial: This explicitly repeats the existential-import problem; the rendering does not erase the difference between a complemented predicate and negative predication.

فيكون مرجع التباين الجزئي إلى سالبتين جزئيتين .
لا يقال : ان المباينة الجزئية قسم من النسب مع أنها غير مندرجة في شئ منها فيوجد كليان ليس بينهما احدى النسب الأربع . لأنا نقول : المباينة الجزئية جنس للمباينة الكليّة والعموم من وجه ومنحصرة فيهما فإذا قيل : النسبة بين هذين الكليين اى : المباينة الجزئية ، كان حاصله ان النسبة في بعض الصّور مباينة كلية وفي بعض أخرى عموم من وجه فلم يوجد كليان لا يكون بينهما احدى النسب الأربع . ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
Partial disjointness therefore resolves into two particular negatives.

Do not object that partial disjointness is a kind of relation which falls under none of the four, so that two universals could fail to bear any of the four relations. We answer that partial disjointness is a genus embracing total disjointness and overlap and is confined to those two. To say that the relation between the universals is partial disjointness amounts to saying that in some cases the relation is total disjointness and in others overlap. Thus no pair of universals has been found which fails to bear one of the four relations.
records.editorial: This speaker accepts the genus/species explanation that note13 treated with caution. Both are retained. ‘Two particular negatives’ has its source-specific existential and modal setting.

It is as though someone had said: on this account the four relations must become five, because a further relation—partial disjointness—has arisen. The answer is that partial disjointness is realised within overlap and also within total disjointness. It is therefore not independent, so as to be called a fifth relation.

records.english:
On ‘that is, just as between the contradictories of the broader …’: this removes a possible difficulty. A comparison apparently requires its point of resemblance already to be known in the object with which something is compared, as in ‘Zayd is like a lion.’ Here it is not known: it has not previously been established whether the contradictories of two disjoint terms are partially disjoint. How, then, can the contradictories of overlapping terms be compared with them?

The answer is that, as the rhetoricians explain, a comparison's purpose may concern either the thing compared or the thing with which it is compared. The stated requirement applies only to the first kind; the present example belongs to the second. Here the relevant characteristic need not previously be known in the comparison's second term. It resembles the verse, ‘Dawn appeared, its bright brow like the caliph's face when he is praised.’ Dawn's brightness and radiance are compared with the caliph's face, although that characteristic had not previously been established of his face. This is called an inverted comparison: what is really being compared in the verse is the caliph's face, and here it is the contradictories of disjoint terms. The comparison has been reversed to suggest that their possession of the characteristic is greater. Reflect. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

records.english:
‘This’ may be the predicate of a suppressed subject, giving ‘the matter is this,’ or a subject with a suppressed predicate, giving ‘this is as stated.’ Alternatively hā may be an imperative verbal noun meaning ‘take,’ with dhā as its object. Or hā may be an attention particle, with an imperative understood: ‘take,’ according to the usual explanation, or ‘know,’ as suggested by the subsequent ‘and know also.’

This is an abrupt transition approaching a skilful transition, like the Qurʾānic words following the description of the people of Paradise: ‘This; and for the transgressors there is an evil return.’ The author reports Ibn al-Athīr as saying that ‘this’ in such a position effects a separation better than a conjunction: it forms a strong connection when leaving one discourse for another. He then calls it a division of discourse better than a smooth transition.

It follows that the claim in some marginalia that ‘this’ is the grammatical subject of ‘is correct’ is inappropriate. It prefers what is unpalatable when something agreeable is available; moreover there is no reason to employ an overt demonstrative when a pronoun would suffice. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

records.english:
On ‘the first is the intention of brevity …’: had he explained the contradictories immediately after the positive terms, the greatest possible brevity would have been to say, after ‘if the two universals are wholly separate they are disjoint,’ ‘and their contradictories are partially disjoint’; and then here, after ‘otherwise they overlap,’ ‘and their contradictories are like those of disjoint terms.’ Compare that with the book's actual wording.

You may object: once postponement is chosen, it would be better and shorter to say, ‘Between their contradictories and those of disjoint terms there is partial disjointness,’ avoiding the suggestion of a comparison with something unknown. I reply: coordinating with a pronoun governed by a preposition without repeating that preposition is permitted by some grammarians but not by the majority. The latter also appears to be the author's position in some of his investigations. Reflect.

One investigating glossator adds a third reason: had the author mentioned the contradictories of total disjointness at its original place, his wording would have been repetitive, independently of losing the desired brevity. But, as our proposed wording shows, no such repetition is necessary. If you say that ‘their contradictories’ would still be repeated, I reply that this is not objectionable repetition. The author repeats ‘their contradictories’ in all the other cases, and doing so here would avoid the suspicion of comparing with a case whose rule has not yet been explained. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

records.english:
On ‘insofar as it is abstracted from the specificity of its two instances’: this qualification is needed because, insofar as partial disjointness exists within one of its two kinds, its conception requires only that particular kind.

You may object: a general notion considered as general does not require conceiving any of its instances, still less all of them. Conceiving animal as animal does not require conceiving human, horse or another animal. Likewise partial disjointness, abstracted from its two particular kinds, should not require conceiving either, still less both.

I reply: what is intended is not partial disjointness considered simply in itself, but considered as existing—not within a specified kind, but within an unspecified one. Considered thus, conceiving it does depend upon conceiving the two kinds.

Why did they consider it in this respect rather than simply in itself? Because, as indicated at the beginning, the purpose here is to explain the relations actually obtaining between universals. That is why they restricted them to four, although partial disjointness differs conceptually from those four. When they say that the contradictories of overlapping or disjoint terms are partially disjoint, they mean partial disjointness as realised, without specifying the kind in which it is realised, not merely partial disjointness in itself.

This also exposes the weakness of the objection that the fourfold classification is defective because partial disjointness is conceptually different from the four. The aim is not relations merely in themselves, but relations as realised. Under that consideration partial disjointness is nothing other than overlap or total disjointness, as the glossator has explained. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

records.english:
This answers a possible objection: the externally existing instance of the concept ‘necessary existent’ does not have a universal quiddity under which it falls, although it is a real particular. It would therefore be incorrect to say that every real particular falls under a general concept. The usual answer is to deny that it lacks every such concept: concept, thing and entity are universal concepts, and it falls under each.

That answer, however, rests on looseness of expression. Otherwise God—blessed and exalted—does not fall under any universal quiddity in which another thing shares. Were He to do so, He would be composed of what is shared and what distinguishes Him; He would depend on each component and on another agent composing them, and would thus be originated, as established in theology. Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say.

You may object: it is necessarily known in religion that ‘existent,’ for example, is applied to the eternal God and also to other existents. We answer that this is verbal, not conceptual, community of meaning. The existence belonging to Him differs from that belonging to other created things. The same applies to ‘thing,’ ‘entity,’ ‘concept’ and similar expressions, as sincere reflection reveals; otherwise the previous unacceptable consequence would follow.

Although this is not the place for that discussion, we have indicated it briefly lest a beginner adopt the other account as his doctrine and thereby go astray and mislead others. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.editorial: This is the glossator's theological rejection of shared conceptual predication, not an editorial assertion that all philosophical or theological schools agree.

records.english:
An investigating glossator says: the preceding explanation assumes that the author's pronoun ‘it’ refers to the particular, as is apparent; the present discussion assumes that it refers to ‘the narrower.’ The latter interpretation is remote. The author did not intend to define or explain the relative particular. Were he doing so, he would be defining it by itself if ‘narrower’ meant simply ‘the specific,’ without comparative force. If it retained comparative force, he would define it through something whose conception depends on its conception, since conceiving ‘narrower’ depends on conceiving ‘specific,’ which is the relative particular itself. He intended only to identify what the expression ‘particular’ is applied to; hence the glossator says, ‘The word particular, just as it is applied ….’ No objection arises that needs an answer. The pronoun should therefore refer to the relative particular. End of that glossator's words; may his station be elevated.

I say that al-Sharīf also gives this argument in his marginalia on the commentary on the Risāla in a corresponding case. It shows only that the relative particular cannot be given a real definition through ‘the narrower,’ as both discussions apparently suppose. A real definition must yield the quiddity of the defined thing through the defining quiddities, as in defining human through rational animal. Here the quiddity of ‘narrower’ does not yield that of ‘relative particular’: they are one and the same kind of thing.

Animal and rational, by contrast, differ from human, which is composed of them. Considered individually they are clearer and better known than human as such, and thus yield it. Human as composed of their two quiddities was unknown, while each quiddity separately was known. Conceiving them and their composition therefore yields the human quiddity that had not previously been apprehended.

The argument does not show that a verbal explanation through ‘narrower’ is impossible. If the concepts of relative particular and narrower were identical, such an objection might also be made to verbal explanation; but they are not. At most they have the same external instances, and that is required of a definiens and definiendum. The case is like explaining ghaḍanfar as ‘lion.’ Nothing shows that the present interpretation depends on ‘narrower’ being a real definition of relative particular; it rather appears to be a verbal explanation. Nevertheless, just as a broader term cannot receive a real definition through a narrower one, it cannot receive a verbal definition through it either. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

The statement that tafsīr concerns transmitted reports and taʾwīl concerns indication is an explanation by something narrower. The subtlety of this observation is apparent. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

records.english:
On ‘from it one learns that the particular …’: from the fact that the narrower term meant here is broader than the narrower term discussed earlier, one learns that relative particular is broader than real particular. The narrower term here may be universal or a real particular; it explains ‘relative particular.’ Since the breadth of the explanation entails the breadth of what is explained, one learns that a relative particular may be universal or a real particular. This is the sense in which the relation between the two particulars is learned by implication.

This works if it is a real definition. If it is a verbal explanation, as intended, there is a difficulty: a verbal explanation may be broader, so the breadth of the explaining term does not entail the breadth of the term explained. The desired conclusion is therefore not established. Understand. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

[A separately introduced modern annotation by Muḥammad al-Karmī, cited to al-Taqrīb p.28, follows. Its position is registered but its text is not reproduced here.]

records.english: For a thing to be so ‘in reality itself’ means that it is so according to itself: amr here means the thing. Its existence does not rest on someone's supposition or consideration; it obtains in itself. The connection between sunrise and the existence of daylight, for example, obtains in itself whether or not anyone supposes it, or any supposer exists at all. Reality itself is absolutely broader than external reality: everything externally existent exists in reality itself, but not conversely. It overlaps with the mental, since falsehoods can be considered and believed—for example, that five is even. Such a proposition exists in the mind but not in reality itself. Cases of this kind are called genuinely mental. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

One account derives the name from īsā, ‘universal,’ and ghūjī, ‘five.’ Another says that it was the name of a sage who discovered and systematised them, so they were named after their discoverer. records.english:
Examples are ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible in the general sense of possibility.’ Both are universal concepts, yet neither can really be predicated of an external or mental thing. Whatever is supposed externally or mentally is a thing and is possible; their contradictories therefore cannot be predicated of a concept among concepts. No significant purpose is served by investigating merely hypothetical universals, and they fall outside our inquiry.

The fivefold division is consequently not refuted by definitions and descriptions of nonexistent things. Someone raised such an objection: predicating something of a thing presupposes the existence of the subject; if the subject does not exist, how can one claim that this predicate is essential or accidental to it? We answer that, although universals are all produced through intellectual consideration and abstraction from individuals, intellectual constructions are of two kinds. In one, that from which the concept is abstracted has a basis and reality; in the other, it is sheer invention. A universal is accordingly either abstracted or invented. Essential and accidental are considered in the first kind, not the second.

The writers restricted the discussion of the predicables to simple meanings for the reader's convenience. The five can also be considered in compound meanings; every concept, simple or compound, falls under one of the five. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

records.english:
On ‘the universal, when related …’: an objection is that some universals fall under none of the divisions—for example, thing and existent. They are not species, since every thing and existent has something additional to mere thinghood and existence. They are not genera, since they are not parts of the realities: otherwise what has been designated a highest genus would not truly be highest. Nor are they differentiae, since they are not parts of the quiddities; even if they were, they would constitute the entirety of what is shared. Finally they are not properties or common accidents, since these are accidents, and thing and existent cannot be accidents. Their subject would be either thing and existent, making something accrue to itself, or non-thing and non-existent, making contradictories coincide.

The answer chooses the first alternative without accepting the consequence. Thinghood accrues to what becomes a thing through that attribution, and existence is treated similarly. Thus the alleged self-attribution does not follow. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

records.english:
On ‘if it is the entirety of what is shared’: what is meant is the entirety of what the items share. The article is generic, so the definition covers both a plurality of shared constituents and a single shared constituent. Animal, a composite genus, is the sum of what human and horse share: every shared constituent is part of it. Substance, a simple genus, is the entirety of what intellect and human share: there is no shared constituent other than it.

Some explain the phrase only in the first sense, as ‘all the shared parts,’ giving animal as the totality of substance, body, growth, sensation and voluntary movement shared by human and horse. Their definition then fails to include simple genera.

You may object that the account excludes remote genera, which are only parts of what is shared. Growing body is not the whole shared by human and horse—animal is—and body without qualification is only a part of what they share, or of what they and a tree share. These remote genera would then fall under ‘otherwise it is a differentia.’

I reply that growing body, although not the entirety shared by human and horse, is the entirety shared by human and tree. Likewise body, although not the entirety shared by human and horse or by those and a tree, is the entirety shared by one of them and a stone. Apply the same reasoning elsewhere. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

A separately introduced explanation by Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm follows: ‘The entirety of what is shared’ means a shared constituent beyond which there is no further shared constituent outside it. Everything shared is either that constituent itself or a part of it. Animal is the whole shared by human and horse: every shared constituent is either animal itself or something within it, such as substance, growing body, sensation or voluntary movement. Although each is shared by human and horse, none individually is the whole shared; animal embraces them all.
